sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner draws the same line between the two seats. Matt Krause calls the broker the “kitchen owner”: the broker holds the MC number and surety bond and runs invoicing, carrier pay, compliance and claims. In return, the broker makes 100% of the profit while footing 100% of the risk [xe6QTceV_JE @ 00:01:04]. Nate Cross of Freight 360 describes the same structure. A licensed, usually mid-size brokerage maintains authority, bond and insurance, and the agent works from home as an independent contractor. The back office absorbs billing, collections, claims, cash flow, marketing and IT support, and sometimes pricing and dispatch [SPl9Y_xMJHA @ 00:02:08]. Victor Mason compresses it to one line: the agent is “only the front end,” operating under the brokerage's authority while focusing on sales and relationships. He calls it the lowest barrier to entry in the business [4n9e0eEuFtM @ 00:01:23]. Krause adds the piece new operators underestimate. The brokerage supplies credit to float shippers who pay in 30 to 60 days. It also carries the $75K bond, which costs roughly $1,200 to $1,300 in premium with good credit [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:01:46]. Krause sums up the trade as profit margin for peace of mind: “The broker is building a business and the agent is building a job.”

The second point of agreement is that commission is cut from margin, never from gross. Krause says it flatly: “it's always a percent of the margin” [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:01:29]. Freight 360's commission breakdown repeats the rule: “you should only ever get compensated off of your margin” [e9-lormMK4w @ 00:23:06]. The ranges cluster tightly. Krause puts splits at 50 to 80%, mostly 60 to 70%, with agents who bring their own shippers commanding the high end. Cross quotes 50 to 70%, with the brokerage keeping 30 to 50% to run its back office and for profit [SPl9Y_xMJHA @ 00:02:46]. Connor Harutyunyan, an ALG agent interviewed by Dennis Brown, reports that new agents typically start near 50%. Some shops pay 40%, and tenured high-volume agents reach 60 to 70%. Connor sits at about 67% [jgNUpO0VPws @ 01:03:33]. Freight 360 separates the roles further: a cradle-to-grave agent can earn 70%, a pure freight finder half or less, and a W-2 rep who did not find the customer 5 to 15% of gross profit. Krause also tells operators to ask exactly what comes out before and after the split: load board, software and insurance. Those deductions quietly change the real percentage an agent takes home.

Practitioners also agree on who should take which seat and what to read before signing. Krause's decision rule is simple. With no logistics, sales or brokering experience, start as an agent. With any one of the three, get your own license [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:00:35]. Krause's three-step funnel follows from that rule: work as an agent, build proven customers, then get licensed. The agent path is the training, and the broker path is how you scale. Ownership of the book is the universal checkpoint. Krause warns operators to check who owns the book of business, to watch for 1 to 2 year non-competes, and to get shipper ownership in writing. Mason says to “read the agreement carefully” for non-competes, non-solicits and whether you build your own book [4n9e0eEuFtM @ 00:03:01]. Robert, a TAB agent on Bobby Loads, verified that his customers could transfer before joining. He points to a contract stating that customers stay his [bkrMqfq4evM @ 00:24:50]. Finally, nobody sells this as passive income. Krause calls it a home-office grind with no steady paycheck. Dennis Brown tells owner-operators that the agent seat is doable at 2 to 3 hours a day, or 10 to 15 hours a week, but “It's not a side hustle” [6bYvpf5qJSY @ 00:32:22].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Run the load math the way the practitioners do. Krause's baseline: the shipper pays $2,000 and the carrier gets $1,700. The $300 margin splits 60/40, so the agent pockets $180 and the brokerage $120 [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:00:50]. Mason's version uses a $2,500 shipper rate and $2,000 in carrier pay. That leaves a $500 margin, and a 50% split pays $250 a load. Two loads a day equals $500 a day, with no cap but no floor either: “If you don't sell, you don't earn” [4n9e0eEuFtM @ 00:02:08]. Connor's example runs smaller. A $1,000 load with $800 to the carrier leaves $200 profit, and a new 50% agent takes $100 [jgNUpO0VPws @ 01:03:51]. Krause's beginner example prices a $500 carrier cost plus 20% for a $100 margin, leaving the agent $60 to $70 [pXxS5GOHXZE @ 00:04:04]. Scale is where the seats diverge. In the same breakdown, Krause models one shipper at 5 loads a week. That pays the agent $900 a week against $1,500 for an owner. At five shippers, it pays the agent $4,500 against $7,500 for the owner. The agent stays ahead at low volume, because the owner's gross must first cover bond premium, a factoring cut, insurance, load board and software before any of it becomes real take-home.

The owner seat carries a cost stack and a cash-flow trap the agent never touches. Krause lists owner startup at $2,500 to $3,500 all-in, including the $300 federal filing and a $20 to $100 process agent. Recurring costs follow: bond premium of $900 to $2,500 a year, plus factoring cuts, insurance, load board and software. The agent's startup is roughly $0, possibly a background check [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:08:29]. The real trap is receivables. Krause walked away from more than $2M in awarded freight because the shipper paid in about 65 days, and neither the factoring company nor a bank would fund it: “I was literally winning too much freight too soon” [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:02:58]. That float is exactly what an agent rents from the brokerage. Dennis Brown adds that a broker can only run one factoring company because of the UCC filing, so that choice locks in early [wOYj-TrF9aI @ 00:32:14]. On margin expectations, Brown analyzed $70B in 2024 freight spend across the top 100 brokerages and found an average margin of 14.99%. He adds that brokers sometimes lose $100 to $500 on a load to keep a client [6bYvpf5qJSY @ 00:10:08]. Krause's year-one owner target lands in the same band: about $300K in business at a 15 to 20% margin.

The agent's paycheck runs on an activity engine. Krause sets the baseline at 100 activities a day. That should yield 10 to 15 decision-maker conversations a week and 1 to 3 quotes. Beginners start at 5 a day and add 5 daily [yeFtuLvEdO8 @ 00:03:43]. Robert, the TAB agent, makes 200 to 600 calls a day and says it takes 5 to 6 touches over 6 to 8 months to win a customer. Robert usually clears $100 to $200 a load and holds a $100 minimum. In August, Robert moved 186 loads for earnings “just above” five figures [bkrMqfq4evM @ 00:16:30]. Carl's surgical prospecting, shown on Krause's channel, cuts the dial count. 100 generic calls produce 2 quotes and 0 loads. 50 targeted calls produce 4 quotes and 1 load at a $200 margin, worth $4,000 a month [EJYdmoWKsmw @ 00:06:34]. Connor went the other way on channel. LinkedIn produced nothing for about a year. Then daily posts about the niche, life and jokes, plus 1,000 to 2,000 targeted connections, turned cold calls into warm ones. The first inbound lead moved three or four shipments the next day [jgNUpO0VPws @ 00:11:52]. Connor's first $10K commission month came after 4 to 5 months, with zero sales background.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The split number is the loudest fault line, and the ranges barely overlap. Matt Krause quotes agent splits of 50 to 80 percent, mostly landing at 60 to 70, with the high end reserved for agents who bring their own shippers, and tells agents to ask exactly what gets deducted before and after the split, from load board to software to insurance [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:04:19]. Nate Cross at Freight 360 pins the agent band at 50 to 70 percent, with the brokerage keeping 30 to 50 to fund the back office and profit [SPl9Y_xMJHA @ 00:02:46]. A separate Freight 360 episode pushes back hard: a cradle-to-grave agent may see 70 percent, but a pure freight finder makes half or less, and that speaker has never seen anything above 50, with most deals at 25 to 40 percent [e9-lormMK4w @ 00:24:30]. Connor Harutyunyan, an ALG agent, splits the difference with real numbers: new agents typically start around 50 percent, some shops pay 40, tenured high-volume agents earn 60 to 70, and Connor personally sits near 67 percent [jgNUpO0VPws @ 01:04:08]. The operator read: the percentage is negotiated off tenure, volume, and whether the agent owns the customer relationship end to end.

Who owns the book is the second split, and Matt Krause contradicts Matt Krause. In one breakdown, an agent who leaves a brokerage gets to keep their clients and carry them to another shop [pXxS5GOHXZE @ 00:04:45]; in another, Krause warns that the agreement decides who owns the book, flags 1-to-2-year non-competes, then tells agents to run a walk-away test and get shipper ownership in writing [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:06:43]. Eagle Express sells the opposite contract outright: no non-compete, so 'your hard work will always belong to you,' paired with a pitch of 100 percent of profit margins, though the same offer carries a 5 percent admin fee on gross and requires transferring an active book [952lbvkEVvM @ 00:00:32]. Robert, a TAB agent on Bobby Loads, says the TAB contract keeps customers with the agent, but insists you verify your customers can transfer before you sign anything [bkrMqfq4evM @ 00:24:50]. The W-2 seat sits at the far pole, where the house owns the accounts outright. The working rule across these speakers: read the non-compete and non-solicit language, and confirm customer portability in writing, before the first dial.

Prospecting splits between raw volume and precision, and follow-up cadence splits even harder. Carl, the 24-year-old running a $6M annualized book on Matt Krause's channel, rejects the spray: 100 generic calls yield two quotes and zero loads, while 50 targeted calls yield four quotes and one load at a $200 margin, roughly $4,000 a month [EJYdmoWKsmw @ 00:06:34]. Once a shipper is won, Carl calls every one weekly on Thursdays, visits quarterly, and keeps the talk about 75 percent personal [EJYdmoWKsmw @ 00:28:24]. Dennis Brown opposes weekly touches on prospects, telling brokers to ask permission to follow up in 30, 60, or 90 days and then do exactly what the prospect said, because calling weekly makes you look like 'a jerk' [wOYj-TrF9aI @ 00:19:36]. Connor Harutyunyan skipped cold volume almost entirely: daily LinkedIn posts, 1,000 to 2,000 targeted connections in year one, direct messages, then phone calls, while dismissing mass email to bought lists of 800 to 1,000 a day as useless because 99 percent lands in spam [jgNUpO0VPws @ 00:36:03]. The reconciling detail is the audience: Carl's weekly rhythm serves existing shippers, Dennis's 30-60-90 rule serves prospects, so retention and prospecting run on separate clocks.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The trap that hits new owners first is cash, not sales. Matt Krause walked away from more than $2M in awarded freight because the shipper paid in about 65 days and neither the factoring company nor a bank would fund it: 'I was literally winning too much freight too soon' [hhT4X32MspU @ 00:03:28]. That squeeze is the core of the agent argument, because the brokerage carries the $75K bond, the back office, and the credit to float shippers who pay in 30 to 60 days. Dennis Brown adds a structural limit on the owner side: a broker can only run one factoring company because of the UCC filing, a point Dennis says they are '98% sure' about [wOYj-TrF9aI @ 00:32:14]. Agents feel a softer version of the same lag. Robert at TAB is paid every 30 days, the first check took 45 days, and TAB offered to split checks to bridge the gap [bkrMqfq4evM @ 00:29:40]. Malcolm Harris on FreightWaves sets the timeline expectation most newcomers skip: an 18-to-24-month minimum ramp, with the reminder that 'you have to buy your seat' before a desk carries its own weight [OHagUq3qWcQ @ 00:38:49].

The second cluster is self-inflicted operating mistakes. Robert calls hiring too soon 'the biggest mistake that we made' and now works alone [bkrMqfq4evM @ 00:12:22]. Robert also runs flat rates with no fuel surcharge and labels that a mistake, while competitors running $25 margins keep pressing on a $100 floor. Dennis Brown sees the same overreach at the brokerage level: a new authority built only to run agents has a 'slim to none' chance, and Dennis spent about three years building an inside team first [jgNUpO0VPws @ 00:54:13]. On freight selection, Dennis warns beginners off fresh produce and deep-frozen loads held at minus 10, since older reefers struggle to hold that temperature in 100-degree Arizona compared with 20-degree Montana [wOYj-TrF9aI @ 00:08:03]. Matt Krause shows what the bad day looks like on a home desk: 100 emails, 10 missed calls, and a truck fire destroying a 40,000 lb ice cream load, followed by 49 or 50 rejections out of every 50 dials [wxTvTywQET4 @ 00:00:54]. None of these failures came from weak demand; each came from scaling headcount, pricing, or freight type ahead of the operator's skill and cash.

The agent-side failure is usually quiet attrition. Connor Harutyunyan lost customers in 2024, fell to zero, and nearly quit, after a first year in which LinkedIn produced nothing; what pulled Connor back was watching other brokers move loads daily and concluding 'That's mean I am slow' [jgNUpO0VPws @ 00:16:42]. Dennis Brown's prescription in the same interview was a 30-day daily-posting challenge, on the logic that 'it cost you zero' and virality is not the goal. Victor Mason names the pattern directly: most people fail because they are inconsistent, and if you don't sell, you don't earn [4n9e0eEuFtM @ 00:03:19]. Contract math is the other quiet leak. Eagle Express advertises 100 percent of profit margins yet takes a 5 percent admin fee on gross, a fee that sits in tension with the headline claim [952lbvkEVvM @ 00:01:19]. Freight 360 adds the fraud tax: double brokering is massive enough that withholding pickup numbers until a carrier is verified by GPS or photo is now industry best practice, delivered through a 'company policy' line, while lying about pickup times is called totally wrong [e9-lormMK4w @ 00:08:15]. The common thread: commission-only income punishes any gap in activity, fees, or carrier vetting immediately.

chapters.question_prompt: Where do I find shippers, how do I land the first one, and how do I turn one load into a repeat account?
chapters.title: Finding and Winning Shippers
chapters.subtitle: Free lead sources and 30,000-lead lists, the "one shipper away" concept, 10–20 daily touches without cold calling, what shippers really want, saturation vs. weak pitches, and live Q&A coaching on landing first freight
chapters.executive_summary: Dennis Brown (Freight Broker Boot Camp, $200M+ brokered 2003-2016), Matt Krause, and Victor Mason converge on one thesis: brokerage is a sales business first, and a startup wins by niching down, building a tight prospect list, and asking for the hardest freight rather than cutting rates. Brown's math says 5-10 small-to-midsize shippers produce six figures; Krause pegs one shipper at 5 loads/week x $200 at $1,000/week and roughly 300 touches per month per yes. The stack is free Apollo, Keychain.com, LinkedIn People tabs, and Lusha for emails, worked through phone, email, LinkedIn, and face-to-face with 8-12 touches to close. They split on volume: Brown pushes 50-75 quality touches daily and 90%+ of time prospecting, while Krause runs 10-20 nightly touches after burning out at 100 a day.

key_metrics.metric: Shippers Needed for a Six-Figure Book

key_metrics.context: Brown puts full-truckload margins at 10-20% and tells new brokers to aim for 10-15% with a $100-per-load minimum.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner here treats shipper acquisition as the whole game. Dennis Brown, who ran a brokerage from 2003 to a 2016 sale and reports $200M+ brokered, frames the business as three moves: find shippers, find carriers, and put profitable loads together, and warns that authority only makes you legal, not profitable [yGyxzLrh7yE @ 00:02:03]. Brown credits niching down for the $200M result and wants the niche picked by equipment, product, lane, or a hybrid such as Midwest steel flatbed [kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:08:37]. Victor Mason lands in the same place, calling brokerage 'a sales business first' and listing what fails: waiting for inbound, 'I'm a broker' posts, generic emails, and chasing every load [8AGIyPDUcqY @ 00:04:16]. On saturation, Brown argues the market is not too crowded; it is 'too saturated with brokers who sound like everybody else,' and brokers who sound identical get picked on price, timing, or incumbency [vvPudiQpMrY @ 00:05:17]. The fix in both camps is focus: flatbed into steel, reefer into food, or Brown's own Northeast outbound van lane. The shared baseline is blunt. A startup does not need thousands of customers like a restaurant or insurance agency; Brown says 5-10 active small-to-midsize shippers produce six figures in profit, so the job is landing a handful of the right accounts, not blasting the whole market with a generic pitch.

The entry wedge everyone repeats is the hard lane. Brown's first-shipper tactic is to ask prospects for their 'difficult or challenging lanes' and prove yourself there; Brown says three struggling salespeople each surfaced new opportunities the same day after one morning meeting and landed first shippers within weeks [57bmm_ipBSY @ 00:01:41]. Hard means awkward pickup or delivery geography, unusual equipment, or multi-pick and multi-drop: Boston to Chicago gets phones ringing 'off the wall,' while Watertown NY to Newark NJ draws 0-2 calls. Brown stresses that challenging freight is not cheap freight; it often pays more because capacity is thin. In the 2026 live Q&A, Brown frames the pitch as 'Give me the hardest stuff,' the 80/20 problem freight [J9NA2KM5qzE @ 00:21:40], and in the 1/19 session says breaking even or losing $100 on that first load is acceptable to get in the door, because 'the hardest part of the whole deal is just moving that first shipment' [j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:44:22]. Matt Krause runs the same play through the backup-number line, and Brown's saturation talk agrees: become the backup option rather than trying to rip out the incumbent [vvPudiQpMrY @ 00:07:06]. The reason is trust. Shippers keep existing brokers and carriers for years, prospects don't trust a newcomer, and Brown's line is that the biggest challenge most brokers have is not price, it's trust.

The third consensus point is that cheap rates are a trap. Brown calls cheapest pricing a 'surefire way to go broke' and teaches showing the real cost of bad service: a lost $1M/year customer costs that amount over 5-15 years [kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:15:02]. The FreightBrokers shipper-wants breakdown says cheap rates get attention but don't keep business, and replaces them with four A's: accuracy on quotes, pickup and delivery times, and paperwork; accessibility, where answering mid-day or at night puts you ahead of 90%; accountability; and authority built through content, podcasts, events, and LinkedIn [JKxqqgS6OBg @ 00:01:18]. Krause, in the $0-$10K system, pushes the same value framing with the land-and-expand question, 'What are the consequences when a carrier falls off your loads?' after overcommunicating on early loads [su_azzEYWO4 @ 00:05:19]. Mason's five steps end on 'be useful,' and treat outreach as starting a conversation, not closing one [8AGIyPDUcqY @ 00:02:07]. Everyone agrees follow-up is where deals actually happen. Brown puts the B2B norm at 8-12 touches, calls 6-8 reasonable, and says a close never happens on the first call. Outreach runs across four channels at once: phone, email, LinkedIn, and face-to-face, with testimonials from existing shippers moving a prospect from fear to trust, and meals or office visits deepening the relationship once a conversation opens.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The list-building stack is almost entirely free. Brown routes students to Apollo through freightbrokerbootcamp.com/freeleads, no credit card, filterable by industry, company size, geography, and job title [j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:11:04], and in the 2026 session says to build a 100-1,000 prospect list before outreach [J9NA2KM5qzE @ 00:19:45]. A worked Apollo search from the August 2025 live: produce companies with 10-100 employees in GA, FL, AL, and NC, filtered to shipping managers, a job Hoovers used to charge about $15k a year for. The Keychain.com walkthrough adds a CPG source: free email signup, 30,000 manufacturers, 2,315 categories, 1M+ products [HeiPAKWzLsI @ 00:02:14]. Search 'ice cream,' get 86 co-manufacturers and 319 packaging suppliers, pull a target such as Pierre's Ice Cream in Cleveland, enrich revenue and main phone in Apollo, open the company's LinkedIn People tab to find the transportation manager, then pull the email with the free Lusha Chrome plugin. Krause builds the list differently: one trailer type, a 30-mile circle, and an AI prompt for 40 manufacturers that skips retailers, distributors, and Fortune 500, then verifies dock doors on satellite view because AI hallucinates [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:05:52]. Plants hiring forklift drivers or importing containers go to the top; shippers with their own trailers drop to the bottom. The target person is whoever gets the call when a truck is late.

Outreach starts with a hook, not a script. Brown says generic 'save you money' scripts die in the first 15 seconds and force two or three hundred dials a day just to find a few people willing to let you quote [UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:38:01]. On LinkedIn, Brown's rule is 'LinkedIn is not Tinder': optimize the profile as a niche expert, never pitch on connect, and post niche content 2-5 times a week; Brown reports $20M+ in annual recurring revenue sourced from LinkedIn and says 15 minutes a day of posting is enough [JTrml3aFNrY @ 00:10:53]. Krause ignores about 90% of pitch-paragraph connection requests, so Krause sends a blank request, offers the network, and after 2-3 messages asks for a 10-minute call, then uses the backup-number line; door two is a 40-second face video, door three a warm path to industrial-park neighbors [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:12:16]. When a meeting lands, Brown calls it a buying signal: prepare 3-4 strategic questions, open with 'not even sure if I can help you,' say you are not displacing current providers, talk tracking or vetting only when asked, and book the next call before hanging up [3NBT5XIIshA @ 00:12:34]. On ghosting, never send 'just checking in'; use sales intelligence and stretch follow-ups out to 2-4 weeks.

The numbers are tight and specific. In the 2026 live Q&A, Brown puts full-truckload margin at 10-20%, or $100-200 per $1,000 of revenue, averaging 15-17%, and tells newcomers to start at 10-15% [J9NA2KM5qzE @ 00:32:50]. In the 1/19 session Brown adds that 'complexity creates margin': multi-stop, pads and straps, or expedited service lifts thin niches like lumber and recycling back to 10-15%, and any shipper that can't clear $100 gross per load gets dropped [j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:28:47]. Krause's side-hustle math: one shipper at 5 loads a week x $200 is $1,000 a week, roughly 300 touches a month may produce one yes, and five shippers reach $5,000 a week [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:02:21]. In the $0-$10K system, Krause anchors on 3-5 clients and a 'golden lane' at 12-16% (also stated as 12-18%); at $300 a load you need 33 loads a month, Atlanta to Dallas three times weekly is $900 a week or over $46K a year, and three golden lanes reach $10K a month [su_azzEYWO4 @ 00:04:01]. Cash timing sits underneath all of it: shippers quote 30 days but pay in 35-45, carriers expect payment in under 30, which is why startups factor, and Brown puts a slow payer on credit hold at 60 days.

callout.title: Street-Level Moves That Shortcut the First Shipper
callout.body: Small plays the practitioners use to turn existing freight, objections, and calendar time into new shipper accounts.
items: Warm-call consignees you already deliver to and attach a testimonial from your shipper; Brown calls that combination a 'slam dunk' [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:24:18].
Answer the 'we're customer-routed' brush-off by asking about inbound freight, returns, and stalled customer pickups, give it 30-60 seconds, then move on [FreightBrokers — UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:41:32].
Skipping Mondays and Fridays cuts 40% of prospecting time; Brown says startup brokers and agents should spend 90%+ of their time prospecting [FreightBrokers — S0a8FejhkCA @ 00:48:08].

sop_steps.title: Lock the Niche and Build the List
sop_steps.action: Pick one equipment, product, or lane niche, then pull 100-1,000 prospects from free Apollo filtered to shipping, logistics, and transportation managers.
sop_steps.detail: Brown says LinkedIn alone is slow, so niche down first (Brown's was Northeast outbound van), then build the list with free Apollo [FreightBrokers — J9NA2KM5qzE @ 00:17:04].

sop_steps.title: Write the Hook and Role-Play It
sop_steps.action: Replace the generic 'save you money' script with a niche-specific hook, then rehearse it daily until it holds past the first 15 seconds.
sop_steps.detail: Brown prescribes role-playing an hour a day for a week or more, recording the sessions, and self-critiquing before going live [FreightBrokers — dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:55:26].

sop_steps.title: Run Daily Multichannel Touches and Log Them
sop_steps.action: Work phone, email, LinkedIn, and face-to-face touches every session and record each one in a tracking sheet.
sop_steps.detail: Krause logs every touch in an 8-column sheet and diagnoses with three numbers: many rows with few replies means fix the opener or targeting, replies without calls means fix the call-ask [Matt Krause — NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:19:57].

sop_steps.title: Ask for the Hardest Lane, Then Send the Packet
sop_steps.action: Offer to cover the prospect's difficult lanes, move the first load even at break-even, and send the broker-shipper agreement and credit app only after commitment.
sop_steps.detail: Brown defines hard lanes by pickup or delivery geography, unusual equipment, or multi-pick and multi-drop, and says that approach worked virtually every time [FreightBrokers — 57bmm_ipBSY @ 00:02:57].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Touch volume is the sharpest split. Dennis Brown attacks the generic dialer model head-on: a canned 'save you money' script dies in the first 15 seconds, which forces a rep to make two or three hundred calls a day just to find a few people willing to let them quote [UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:38:01]. Brown's replacement is 50 to 75 quality, multichannel touches a day across phone, email, LinkedIn and face-to-face, calling it a combination of quality and quantity that beats 150 to 200 generic dials [3NBT5XIIshA @ 00:40:35]. Matt Krause cuts the number far lower for anyone still holding a job: 10 to 20 touches in a two-hour evening block, roughly eight minutes per prospect, enough time to find the right person and send something that does not read like copy-and-paste [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:01:48]. Krause tried 100 a day, which works out to one touch every 72 seconds, and burned out on it. Krause's payoff math still runs on volume over time: about 300 touches a month may produce one yes, and one shipper at five loads a week and $200 a load is $1,000 a week [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:02:21]. The operator takeaway: Brown sets a full-time daily floor, while Krause builds a nightly side-hustle cadence and lets monthly totals compound.

LinkedIn splits the room even inside Brown's own catalog. The bullish version: Brown credits LinkedIn with over $20 million in annual recurring revenue between 2003 and 2016, and prescribes 15 minutes a day of posting images, short stories, tips and shipment examples, pointing to Jason Rabine posting daily to 11,373 followers [JTrml3aFNrY @ 00:13:06]. The 2026 version is colder: LinkedIn alone is slow, so niche down first, build a 100 to 1,000 prospect list in free Apollo, and run all four channels, with email getting filtered and LinkedIn reserved for dialogue rather than cold pitching [J9NA2KM5qzE @ 00:17:04]. Krause agrees pitching on connect fails but goes further on mechanics: send a blank connection request, offer your network, and only after two or three messages ask for a 10-minute call; Krause ignores roughly 90% of the pitch-paragraph requests that land in their own inbox [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:09:02]. Brown's line is that LinkedIn is not Tinder and it is social selling, not cold calling [dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:08:27]. Where they part ways is the next move: Brown pushes profile optimization and two to five niche posts a week, while Krause's next doors are a 40-second face video and warm introductions to industrial-park neighbors.

The entry offer splits too. Brown's first-shipper play is to ask for the prospect's hardest lanes, the problem freight a carrier or broker hands back last-minute, and to accept breaking even or losing $100 on that first load just to get in the door [j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:42:43]. Brown frames challenging freight as often more expensive, not cheaper, because capacity is thinner and complexity is higher. Krause builds around the opposite end of the book: a golden lane, the single most repeatable lane at 12 to 16% margin (also stated as 12 to 18%), where Atlanta to Dallas three times a week at $300 a load is $900 a week and three such lanes reach $10K a month [su_azzEYWO4 @ 00:03:23]. Both still land on complexity as the margin engine, with Krause naming heavy haul, high-value reefer and time-sensitive freight. Targeting order differs as well. Brown niches by equipment, product, lane or a hybrid such as Midwest steel flatbed, and Brown's own origin niche was Northeast outbound van [yGyxzLrh7yE @ 00:07:06]. Krause reverses the sequence: pick one trailer type and a 30-mile circle, rank the plants inside it, then ask each plant where its freight goes rather than choosing a lane first [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:04:45].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap Brown reports is credit, not sales. Shippers quote 30-day terms but actually pay in 35 to 45 days, carriers expect money in under 30, and anyone pushing 90-day terms gets avoided, which is why most startups run on factoring [dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:17:49]. Brown calls cash flow king for a broker, self-funded the original brokerage, and still notes that most students who reached six to eight figures used factoring before weaning off it [kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:28:15]. Brown also disputes claims that 90 to 120 days is normal and puts the typical range at 30 to 60 days. The enforcement side is blunt: Brown fired seven-figure clients for paying late, puts a shipper on credit hold at 60 days, and points to AR insurance with roughly a $10K deductible as the backstop [UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:49:01]. The cautionary case is a student who skipped credit checks and is now owed $100K, being paid back $10K at a time; Brown's fix is to state 30-day terms upfront and call the shipper's payables contact right after the first invoice [dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:50:30]. Brown's survival line is that profit is required, but a brokerage that pays its bills and runs at break even can sustain itself forever.

The second trap is competing on price or fishing in the wrong pond. Brown calls the cheapest-rate strategy a surefire way to go broke and reframes the pitch around the real cost of bad service: a shipper who loses a $1M-a-year customer to bad service loses that amount over five to fifteen years [kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:15:02]. On marketplaces, Brown is categorical: uShip and Freightos attract cheap shippers, they are a waste of time, and Brown has never seen a broker or agent build a successful brokerage or agency from those platforms [S0a8FejhkCA @ 00:45:28]. The saturation complaint gets the same diagnosis. Brown argues freight brokerage is not too saturated; it is saturated with brokers who sound like everybody else, so shippers choose them on price, timing or incumbency, and brokers fail from lack of focus, training, sales skill and consistency [vvPudiQpMrY @ 00:05:17]. Victor Mason lists what reliably does not work in the field: waiting for inbound, generic 'I'm a broker' posts, generic emails and chasing every load, because brokerage is a sales business first [8AGIyPDUcqY @ 00:03:12]. Mason's counter is outreach built to start a conversation, not close it, followed by follow-up and being useful.

The third cluster is self-inflicted pipeline damage. Krause's volume fallacy produces 14-hour days, and the fix is 80/20: three to five anchor clients who trust you with their core freight [su_azzEYWO4 @ 00:00:35]. Krause's diagnostic uses three numbers from an eight-column touch log: many rows and few replies means the first message or targeting is broken, replies without calls means the call-ask line is broken, and only 60 rows means the system was not run enough nights; margin is still not take-home pay once bond, software and taxes come out [NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:20:29]. Brown's follow-up rules ban 'just following up' and 'just checking in,' stretch ghosted follow-ups to two to four weeks using sales intelligence, and require booking the next call before hanging up; mass automation of 10,000 emails or 500 LinkedIn messages a day does way more damage [3NBT5XIIshA @ 00:32:48]. Success breeds its own trap: when loads pile up and prospecting stops, the business dies, so Brown's fix is to hire operations help, hand off about 50% of that work and keep selling, because B2B deals take eight to twelve touches and never close on the first call [kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:39:40].

callout.title: Four Checks Before a New Shipper Gets a Second Load
callout.body: Brown and Krause both lost time or money where credit, margin, vetting and prospecting discipline slipped. Clear each check before scaling volume with any new account.
items: Terms and payables: 30-day terms stated upfront, the shipper's accounts-payable contact called after the first load, and credit hold triggered at 60 days unpaid [FreightBrokers — dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:50:30].
Margin floor: after the deliberate break-even first load, every load clears $100 gross and new brokers target 10-15%; shippers below $100 gross get dropped [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:27:30].
Vetting: proper due diligence completed on the shipper, the carrier and the driver before the load is tendered [FreightBrokers — UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:34:40].
Pipeline: 90% or more of a startup's time stays on prospecting even as loads arrive, because the business dies when prospecting stops [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:49:18].

chapters.question_prompt: What do I actually say on a cold call to a shipping manager, and how do I handle the objections that end the call?
chapters.title: Cold Calling That Books Freight
chapters.subtitle: Scripts and 6-step call structure, lessons from 23,000 cold calls, tone and pacing, "we don't use brokers" and other objections, live call breakdowns, post-first-load follow-up scripts, and how cold calls plus service built a $50M brokerage
chapters.executive_summary: Phone-built freight brokers agree on the fundamentals: dial daily (Dennis Brown sets 50 calls as the floor), sell reliability and trust instead of the lowest rate, listen far more than you talk, stand up, and rehearse by recording yourself. The street mechanics are precise. Brown opens with "you're most likely going to hate me, I'm a freight broker," while Matt Krause asks for help and cites Gong data showing "did I catch you at a bad time" books under 1%. Objections get scripted answers, pauses, and diagnostic questions; one "we don't use brokers" prospect became a $150 test load and roughly $20,000 a year in profit. Practitioners split on the close: Krause asks only for a saved backup number, Freight 360 asks for the business on call one, and Sales Scripter books a second meeting.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here treats the phone as the front door to shippers and prospecting as non-negotiable daily work. Dennis Brown sets 50 calls a day as the minimum baseline and warns that brokers who stop prospecting stop growing [BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:33:36]. Matt Krause, who logged roughly 23,000 rejections on the way past seven figures, calls cold calling "very much still alive" and frames it as problem-solving inside "a big numbers game," where prospects reject the offer rather than the caller and every no counts as a gym rep [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:08:06]. Krause's later script math is blunt: 29 of 30 calls end in a no, and "boring is the point" [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:34:03]. John Ferguson built Pivot Supply Chain Solutions the same way, scraping about 30,000 leads during a 24-hour NAICS trial and planning to dial 150 a day to clear the list in a month [PyjJOzy-a2s @ 00:09:33]. The shared baseline is detachment backed by volume. Krause argues the less you need any single deal, the more you close, and urges an abundance mindset because tens of thousands of US shippers exist. Desperation, in this camp, is the real enemy, not the dial count.

The second point of agreement is that price does not win shippers, and leading with cheap rates is a trap. Krause says competing on lowest rates left razor-thin margins and clients who walked the moment a competitor undercut, so the pitch shifted to on-time delivery, reliability, and communication, and price-only shippers got dropped [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:01:55]. Dennis Brown states flatly that "price is not the number one objection," explaining that being $10 to $100 high is not a pricing problem while being 30% high is, and the real gap is trust [90xG4lQaA6Q @ 00:32:15]. Brown names the root fear: "the biggest reason why shippers don't do business with new brokers is fear of the unknown" [BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:32:50]. The pet food case on the FreightBrokers channel shows trust in action: the prospect's "we don't use brokers" was an escape button because another broker had burned her, and the cure was proof of after-hours accountability plus a customer testimonial [knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:01:01]. Brown treats the first load as a test: shippers score pickups, deliveries, damage claims and rejected loads, so the move is to under-promise and over-deliver to climb from one load to ten a day.

On delivery, the practitioners converge almost word for word. Benjamin Kowalski of Freight 360 says "god gave you two ears and one mouth," so listen twice as much as you talk, follow every statement with a question, and mirror the prospect's tone and pace, fast in New York and slower in the South [ImGEvDRAqaw @ 00:04:56]. Kowalski also wants reps standing, because "motion creates emotion," and smiling at a mirror above the phone. Krause runs the same playbook: stand up and smile, with a sticky note as a reminder, and mirror the prospect's pace while offering a callback if they are busy [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:12:56]. Krause's guide says 99% of reps over-talk and that a call should stay under five minutes [6yGrLWuRK6g @ 00:05:25]. Recording is the other shared drill. Brown's main cold calling tip is to role-play the call and record it, rehearsing each common objection 20 to 50 times and using playback to fix pace, tonality, verbal tics and over-talking [90xG4lQaA6Q @ 00:07:03]. Krause's own drill is identical: record, check speed and pitch, then re-record. Across these sources, the voice on the line is treated as the product before any lane gets quoted.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The opener is where the mechanics get specific. Dennis Brown says the hardest part of a cold call is the first 5 to 15 seconds, and retires stale lines like "trucks in your area," "save you money," and "network of over 10,000 trucks" as delivering very low return on investment. Brown's replacement, adapted from a sales-training call Brown personally received, runs: "hey John, John this is Dennis, you're most likely going to hate me, I'm a freight broker, so do you want to hang up now or will you give me 30 seconds to tell you why I'm calling" [-_16MS3HWhA @ 00:04:17]. A yes buys 30, 60 or 90 seconds for a hook built on market intelligence and a request for a quick follow-up call. Krause kills yes/no openers like "is now a good time?" because 9.5 out of 10 times the answer was "in the middle of something," and instead asks, with no name intro, whether the prospect might help with "something transportation related by chance" [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:03:25]. Krause backs this with Gong data: "did I catch you at a bad time" books under 1%, 40% worse than average, while naming the reason upfront roughly doubles the odds [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:09:19]. One researched nugget mentioned inside the first ten seconds, Krause adds, beats "99.9%" of callers [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:14:32].

Objection handling is scripted down to the pause. On the pet food account, the answer to "we don't use brokers" was "Good. I'm glad to hear it," then silence, then: "several of my customers said the exact same thing... Do you want to know why they eventually decided to work with us?" [knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:01:28]. The ask was one test load with no lane replacement and no commitment; it arrived within about two weeks at roughly $1,500 revenue and $150 gross profit, and a post-delivery "When's the next load on that lane shipping?" won the next one on the spot [knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:04:03]. Krause's NEPQ playbook handles "we're happy" with "I'm not quite sure if we'd even be the right fit for you yet," a 2 to 3 second pause, and a frequency question about how often carriers fall off a load last minute [ZG3bMHTCx1Y @ 00:03:18]. For "send me your rates," Krause warns that giving a number puts you "in a bidding war," so reframe around lead times, appointments and late penalties, then ask for the biggest operational challenge. In the longer script, Krause sorts objections into reflex (agree, then ask), wound (label it) and deflection (take it literally and add one question), noting "none of those is a no" [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:17:41].

The follow-up and the math close the loop. Krause defines the first call's only goal as becoming the broker the shipper would take a second call from, with the number saved as backup, then sends a one-paragraph email within the hour and holds the setup packet (agreement, W9, insurance) until there is a load [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:32:07]. Krause's volume target is 30 to 50 touches a day full-time or 10 to 20 part-time, not 100 dials, and 800 touches a month yields about 25 backup slots; one shipper at five loads and $200 margin is $1,000 a week, five shippers $5,000 [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:35:38]. Dennis Brown's unit economics run $150 to $250 profit per load, startup costs recovered in 10 to 20 loads, and $4,000 a month from 20 loads at $200 [BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:41:03]. Once a load books, Krause's two-paragraph handover email names the carrier, roughly 2:00 p.m. Central pickup, 53-foot dry van, driver Carlos and the driver's direct number, then asks about loads in the next week or two "before things get tight," aimed at the claim that over 80% of brokers lose repeat business after the first load [Bdydc4rCcVs @ 00:00:00].

callout.title: Research and Targeting Edges
callout.body: Targeting tricks the practitioners use to walk into every dial with something specific to say.
items: Scan Google Maps satellite view for buildings with multiple docks and identify the business type: food processors suggest reefer and tight windows, plastics suggest flatbed or oversize [Matt Krause — AWq6iXM53f8 @ 00:14:06]
Photograph product labels with name and address at a supermarket, BJ's or Walmart; shelf goods that are not frozen or refrigerated usually ship in vans [FreightBrokers — BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:22:16]
Work the SONAR tender rejection hot list each morning and open with "I see that your market is experiencing high volume tender rejections, how can I help" [FreightWaves — iOTP-SdRDb4 @ 00:48:53]
Use cold calls just to harvest names: ask for shipping, then ask the contact's name before the transfer goes through [eCarrierCheck — gwNcz_V8JZ0 @ 00:03:39]

sop_steps.action: Pull the contact name, company, what it does, and one possible need before dialing.
sop_steps.detail: Krause looks for a new plant, product launch or product change, accepts that about 80% of the time little turns up, and dials anyway [Matt Krause — 6yGrLWuRK6g @ 00:02:38].

sop_steps.action: Use a transparent opener that hands the prospect a choice and buys 30 seconds.

sop_steps.action: Ask one open-ended pain question, then hold a three to five second silence.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The opener is the sharpest split on the floor. Sales Scripter builds its freight script on “Did I catch you in the middle of anything?” followed by a value proposition of best rates and lower costs and a takeaway line, “I don't know if we're a fit” [6W1ym-1hlkc @ 00:00:00]. Matt Krause's six-step guide also asks permission with “out of the blue… quick minute?” and a pitch built as “we help [title] … so you have more time for…” with no features or benefits [6yGrLWuRK6g @ 00:04:12]. Krause then reverses in his longer script breakdown, citing Gong data that “did I catch you at a bad time” books under 1%, roughly 40% worse than average, and swapping it for a request for help plus a pause for a small yes; stating the reason for the call upfront roughly doubles the odds [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:09:19]. Dennis Brown of FreightBrokers runs a third playbook that names the annoyance outright: “you're most likely going to hate me I'm a freight broker so do you want to hang up now or will you give me 30 seconds to tell you why I'm calling” [-_16MS3HWhA @ 00:04:17]. Dennis calls it a pattern interrupt that is authentic, transparent and hands control to the prospect, and writes off “trucks in your area,” “save you money” and “network of over 10,000 trucks” as openers that only work at scale with very low return on investment.

What counts as a win on call one splits four ways. Freight 360's Benjamin Kowalski says always ask for the business, anything on their desk, and calls it the step most rookies forget [ImGEvDRAqaw @ 00:08:24]. Matt Krause sets the bar lower on purpose: the shipper is already covered by carriers, a broker or both, so the only goal is to be the broker they would take a second call from, with the number saved as backup, and never guess a rate on that first conversation [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:01:33]. Sales Scripter's live call closes on neither freight nor a backup slot but on a second conversation: a Detroit-area rep calling within two weeks, accepted after the prospect admitted freight cost was a project for “the next month or so” [sagwYgVmVaE @ 00:01:02]. Dennis Brown splits the difference with a single test load, pitched as no lane replacement and no commitment, after flipping “we don't use brokers” with “Good. I'm glad to hear it” and a proof story about a driver's health emergency transloaded on the fly and still delivered on time [knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:03:27]. That test load arrived in about two weeks at roughly $1,500 revenue and $150 gross profit. Questioning style diverges too: Kowalski arms reps with a prepared list of operational questions, while Krause warns against reading off a list of nine.

Daily volume targets do not line up. Dennis Brown calls 50 calls a day the minimum baseline and says brokers who stop prospecting stop growing [BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:33:36]. Matt Krause pushes back on dial-count culture: 30 to 50 touches a day full-time, 10 to 20 part-time, not 100 dials, with 29 of 30 calls ending in a no and 800 touches a month yielding about 25 backup slots [r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:33:05]. John Ferguson went the other direction launching Pivot Supply Chain Solutions, scraping about 30,000 leads off a 24-hour NAICS trial in 8 hours and planning to call 150 a day to clear the list in a month [PyjJOzy-a2s @ 00:09:33]. On price, Jared of eCarrierCheck calls breaking even, around $50, acceptable to start a relationship, and on a live call fielded a buyer probing whether a $3,000 move could flex to $2,800 or $2,700 [gwNcz_V8JZ0 @ 00:58:15]. Even the weight of relationships is contested. Ferguson opens with “Your customers are all you have” and tells brokers to pick up the phone instead of just sending a quote, while the FreightCaviar host argued relationships may not be essential and that brokers “assume their station” [PyjJOzy-a2s @ 00:57:20]. Ferguson's counter is blunt: an AI bot calling to build relationships is not going to cut it, and voice agents still transfer to humans.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Matt Krause's most expensive lesson was tonal, not tactical: $750 lost on a load won with desperate energy, with no leverage once the market spiked [AWq6iXM53f8 @ 00:00:00]. Early on, 100 calls a day produced about one meaningful conversation and Krause cut rates to roughly break even on loads. Competing on lowest rates delivered razor-thin margins and clients who walked the moment another broker undercut, and five straight days of follow-ups trained prospects to ignore the calls [LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:01:55]. The rate request is its own trap: hand over a number on “send me your rates” and “You are now in a bidding war,” so Krause reframes around lead time, appointment-based delivery and late penalties, then asks for the biggest operational challenge to sit as a consultant, not a vendor [ZG3bMHTCx1Y @ 00:05:13]. Jared's live call with a PVC pipe shipper in Bowling Green showed the same rot from the buyer's side: two carriers kept because they were “always the cheapest,” and bidding wars putting too many trucks on site [gwNcz_V8JZ0 @ 00:21:21]. The symptoms Krause tags as commission breath, speaking fast, ums, upspeak and jumping to price, signal a thin pipeline, and the cure Krause teaches is enough pipeline that power comes from indifference: there to help, not to beg.

The first load is a test, and Dennis Brown says shippers grade it on a scorecard of pickups, deliveries, damage claims and rejected loads [BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:30:49]. Overcommitting is how new brokers flunk it: offered five Buffalo-to-Atlanta loads, take three, because committing to five and covering three makes you “a loser.” The quieter failure is the one Krause calls the ghost broker approach: over 80% of brokers fail to win repeat business after the first load because they send “your load is booked” and vanish, leaving the shipper without the carrier, the phone number or the arrival time, so the shipper starts calling other brokers [Bdydc4rCcVs @ 00:00:17]. The fix is a two-paragraph handover email naming the carrier, pickup window, equipment, driver and the driver's direct line, then a capacity nudge for loads in the next week or two. Dennis's pet food account shows the payoff of the ask: after the first $150 load, “When's the next load on that lane shipping?” won the next one on the spot, and the account grew to about $20,000 a year in profit for 5+ years [knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:04:16]. Kevin Hill of FreightWaves adds a staffing trap: new reps' first freight is often “horrible,” so start them in carrier sales or ops [iOTP-SdRDb4 @ 00:43:49].

Cash and bandwidth break brokerages before the phone does. John Ferguson launched from a basement, invoicing at night, paying carriers via Zelle out of a personal account while customers paid in 30 days, and asked underwriters mid-call for $900 to $1,500 in credit because top loads paid about $2k [PyjJOzy-a2s @ 00:17:55]. Recycling shippers in that early book cared only about rate. Jared of eCarrierCheck admitted on a live call that he failed to ask about payment terms, with fuel at $5 a gallon putting a 300-gallon fill near $1,500 for the carrier, and his verdict on a shipper that won't work with him was “I'd probably find another shipper” [gwNcz_V8JZ0 @ 00:59:07]. Kevin Hill warns that cradle-to-grave service eats selling time: cross-border Mexico work once meant eight hours with no sales calls, which is why Axle's team leaders cover check calls so a rep can “go sell for an hour” [iOTP-SdRDb4 @ 00:36:55]. Dennis Brown flags two more traps: the lowest RFQ bidder often cannot cover the volume and rejects the tender, so placing second to fourth wins, and LinkedIn automation violates terms of service and can cost the account entirely [90xG4lQaA6Q @ 00:46:54]. His bidding rule is to bid only the 20 to 40 lanes you are actually good at.

callout.title: Four checks before the next dial session
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, reversal or bottleneck a practitioner hit on the phones or after the first load. Clear all four before scaling dial volume.
items: Retire the “did I catch you at a bad time” opener; Gong data shows it books under 1%, about 40% worse than average, so ask for help and pause for a small yes instead [Matt Krause — r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:09:19].

Never answer “send me your rates” with a number; that starts a bidding war, so reframe around lead time, appointments and late penalties and ask for the biggest operational challenge [Matt Krause — ZG3bMHTCx1Y @ 00:05:13].
Accept only the loads you can actually cover; take three of five rather than committing to five and covering three [FreightBrokers — BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:36:01].

Send the handover email the moment the carrier is confirmed, with subject line project name, carrier, pickup time, driver and the driver's direct number, or become the ghost broker [Matt Krause — Bdydc4rCcVs @ 00:02:22].

chapters.pull_quote: “Ironically, the less you need any single deal, the more deals you will close.” — Matt Krause (LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:11:15).
action_checklist: Role-play and record the intro plus the four common objections (happy with current provider, send me some info, price too high, don't use brokers), rehearsing each 20 to 50 times [FreightBrokers — 90xG4lQaA6Q @ 00:09:27].
Spend a few minutes at most finding one or two research nuggets, such as a warehouse press release, and mention one within the first 10 seconds of the call [Matt Krause — LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:14:32].
Talk 30% of the time, say questions with a downward inflection, and wait 2 seconds after the prospect stops speaking [Matt Krause — r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:22:24].
Send a one-paragraph email within the hour and hold the setup packet (agreement, W9, insurance) until there is an actual load [Matt Krause — r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:32:07].
On “we don't use brokers,” say “Good. I'm glad to hear it,” stop talking, share why other customers switched, and ask for one test load [FreightBrokers — knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:01:28].
Work shippers first, then brokers, then load boards, and keep calling low-score shippers monthly; one user won a zero-score shipper after six months [eCarrierCheck — gwNcz_V8JZ0 @ 00:46:57].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I price a load, run it through my TMS, invoice it, and make sure cash keeps flowing to me and my carriers?
chapters.title: Quote to Cash: Pricing, Load Operations and Payment
chapters.subtitle: The four key numbers for pricing a first load, DAT/Truckstop rate data, freight pricing AI, how brokers think on rate calls, TMS operations workflows, invoicing and margin, quick pay vs. factoring
chapters.executive_summary: Brokers price from the truck up. They collect every load detail, pull DAT and FreightWaves lane data from several sources, fix an expected buy rate, and only then add margin. ShipLeague quotes about $1,850 on a lane where the truck should take about $1,700 and calls 15% standard. FreightBrokers works four numbers ($1,300 buy, $250 target, $1,550 sell, $1,350 ceiling) and books the truck at $1,325. Every money-side speaker separates gross from net and profit from cash: a $300 gross becomes $225 net, and 30-to-90-day terms force a choice. Quick pay costs 1-5% and covers one broker's loads. Factoring costs roughly 3-5% and advances 80-90% inside 24 hours. Practitioners split on quick pay versus factoring, on which AscendTMS perks are free, and on whether factoring rescues a thin operation or just helps it lose money faster.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every pricing practitioner works backward from the truck. FreightBrokers refuses to touch a number until the pickup and delivery details, appointment times, commodity, weight, equipment, driver assist, extra stops and special instructions are collected, because a firm 6:00 a.m. delivery prices differently than "anytime Friday." The carrier figure (the truck or buy rate) then gets built from lane data, load boards, past company pay and direct carrier calls, never from one source alone [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:00:56]. ShipLeague runs the same play with DAT RateView and FreightWaves. They set granularity to "Market" 99% of the time and fix an expected truck pay before a single dollar of margin goes on top [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:01:22]. Tony's Topics treats DAT's Quick Rate Lookup as the reality check, pulling all-in spot rates by equipment type and holding every offer against the market [wOpAqd5AALo @ 00:02:58]. The second FreightBrokers lesson frames the output: research the lane, the market and the carriers, then quote. The result is two separate agreements, one with the shipper and one with the carrier [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:01:55]. The order of operations never flips. Shipper price equals buy rate plus a deliberate gross profit, and the broker's spread lives between two contracts that are negotiated separately and paid on separate clocks.

Gross margin is not take-home pay. FreightBrokers' worked load has the shipper paying $2,100 and the carrier receiving $1,800. That $300 gross margin is "not necessarily what you actually keep." After roughly $75 of load board, TMS, insurance, bond, phone, accounting and factoring expenses, net lands at $225. The same lesson warns that invoiced is not paid: owe ten carriers and $18,000 leaves the building before the first shipper check clears, because "you can have a load that's profitable on paper and still have a cash flow problem" [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:05:20]. BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS makes the identical point from the carrier seat. Brokers and shippers pay in 30, 45 or 60 days, while fuel, insurance, drivers, truck payments and repairs do not wait. Profit measures sustainability; cash flow measures the ability to pay bills [ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:01:47]. Porter Capital puts standard terms at 30-60 days [iJE2rZFL57E @ 00:00:00]. Bumble Bee Dispatch stretches that to 30-90 days and notes that startup costs drain cash before the first payment ever lands [dTOcCujNdaw @ 00:00:50]. The shared answer is to fund the float through working capital, a credit line, quick pay or factoring, and to price every load knowing none of those options is free money.

Paperwork is the trigger that turns a delivered load into money. FreightBrokers ties both invoices to the proof of delivery. The POD releases the $1,800 carrier invoice and the $2,100 shipper invoice, and any detention, lumper or extra-stop charge needs its own documentation to get paid [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:02:48]. In FreightWaves' Rose Rocket demo, Rob Dougherty automates that hinge: same-day invoicing fires the moment the POD is uploaded and syncs straight to accounting [MobEZyaIjV4 @ 00:04:37]. AscendTMS teaches the same discipline from inside the software. Supporting documents must be uploaded, typed and attached or they sit "unprocessed." Factoring runs through partner companies with an NOA stamp, and a load paid in full earns the "green rectangle of victory" [ICIyOtMiEqY @ 00:24:58]. Steve's longer Ascend training adds that the ready-for-accounting tab is a staging area for collecting paperwork, and that adding an income pay item "is what trips ascend tms to generate an invoice document" [idL8PXMlKjQ @ 00:45:31]. Across a vendor demo, a free TMS and a broker training channel, the operating baseline is identical. No POD means no invoice. No attached document means no payment. The back office runs off load status and logged documents rather than anyone's memory of what happened on the road.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: ShipLeague's worked lane is a van from Atlanta, GA to Vineland, NJ, 766 miles. June ran a $2,183 high and a $1,670 low. The 3-day pull showed a $1,609 average, a $1,678 high and a $1,532 low, but they distrust that dip because the 7-, 15- and 30-day figures sit within $8 of each other, so expected truck pay is about $1,678 [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:02:17]. The market read "+100 very tight" (red is tight, blue is loose). They ignore forecasts and let the 30-day and 7-day data rule. Expecting roughly $1,700 to the truck, they quote about $1,850 and call 15% margin "pretty standard" [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:04:10]. FreightBrokers formalizes the math into four numbers on a Buffalo, NY to Newark, NJ dry van carrying about 22,000 lb of non-stackable furniture. A $1,300 estimated carrier rate plus a $250 target gross profit equals a $1,550 customer rate. With a $200 profit floor, the maximum carrier rate is $1,350 [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:04:26]. The quote goes out as "$1,550" with no apology and no "10-minute song and dance." It states what is included and holds through end of day. The carrier booked at $1,325 for $225 gross [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:06:29], because knowing the ceiling lets the broker negotiate with confidence.

Data access is tiered, and the tier decides what you can see. Tony's Topics lays out DAT's ladder. DAT One Standard carries no lane rates, Enhanced shows a 30-day average, and the other three tiers show 15-day data, so the working minimum is DAT One Pro at $135 a month via Tools > Quick Rate Lookup. Los Angeles to Chicago at 2,025 miles priced van at $1.90 per mile, reefer at $2.21 and flatbed at $2.14, all-in spot [wOpAqd5AALo @ 00:02:14]. ShipLeague's new-lane safety net is "make or break even": price in 150 miles of deadhead so the worst case breaks even, and keep doing it until the lane is learned [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:04:55]. Margin goes up for an undesirable or loose destination, or for freight that is overweight, oversized, tarp-damaging, needs ramps or load levelers, needs driver assist, or loads slowly. Capacity comes from Lane Makers filtered to full truckload, van, 30 days. A carrier that posted the lane nine times gets the "three a month" pitch [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:07:16]. Freight Broker 911 sells the automated version: instant quotes in about 10 seconds built from market data, lane history, fuel and capacity. Pricing is $0 for the first 30 days and stays $0 with an active shipper and at least one shipment per 30 days; otherwise it is $149 a month [edDHTJiH5HM @ 00:00:34].

Inside the TMS, the numbers become documents and deductions. Steve's AscendTMS build sets income at $2.30 per mile, then cuts it to $1.90 per mile for $2,205.90 on 1,161 miles. The carrier gets a flat $1,800 with a $75 extra-stop option, and a 4% quick-pay fee comes off the top: "four percent of 1800 is 72," held back from the carrier's pay [idL8PXMlKjQ @ 00:48:51]. The 2024 Ascend walkthrough shows $3,000 flat income against a $2,000 flat expense, with gross profit and percentage displayed. It auto-generates the bill of lading, carrier confirmation, customer confirmation and invoice. A driver document request texts a link, and the upload attaches straight to the load [Eycc6Jod6t4 @ 00:16:17]. On the payment side, quick pay is priced broker by broker. Trucking From Scratch's David McGill describes 2-, 5- or 14-day tiers, each at a different percentage, with payment instructions printed on the rate confirmation [K9UPJJr_uzQ @ 00:00:17]. Brandon Manney puts broker quick pay at about 2-3% within roughly 7 days, against factoring at 3-5% within 24 hours, which on a $1,000 invoice works out to "$50 plus whatever other fees" [i6KVZJUOBqs @ 00:02:21]. The broker's spread and the carrier's cost of speed get settled on the same invoice.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split in getting paid is quick pay versus factoring, and the practitioners land on different sides depending on how many brokers a truck hauls for. Porter Capital frames quick pay as a 2-to-7-day payout costing 1 to 5 percent, good only for that one broker's loads, and says one broker with solid quick pay may be all a carrier needs while multi-broker scaling calls for factoring [iJE2rZFL57E @ 00:01:14]. David McGill of Trucking From Scratch goes further and prefers factoring outright: twenty to fifty brokers means twenty to fifty invoicing processes, while a factor is one portal or one email, a standardized process that can be delegated to an admin hire, and some brokers do not offer quick pay at all [K9UPJJr_uzQ @ 00:02:43]. Brandon Manney prices the trade-off in plain numbers, quick pay at roughly 2 to 3 percent inside about seven days against factoring at 3 to 5 percent inside 24 hours [i6KVZJUOBqs @ 00:02:21]. Courtney at Bumble Bee Dispatch counters that quick pay is not as cheap as it looks once a 5 percent fee stacks with a $25 to $29 Comchek fee, and steers carriers toward same-day or next-day factoring deposits [dTOcCujNdaw @ 00:04:20].

On pricing, the split is percentage margin versus fixed-dollar margin, and how much data to trust. ShipLeague pulls DAT RateView at Market granularity, ignores forecasts, leans on 30-day and 7-day figures, expects about $1,700 to the truck on a 766-mile Atlanta to Vineland van lane and quotes about $1,850, calling 15 percent margin pretty standard [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:04:10]. FreightBrokers rejects any fixed rule, stating there is no magic profit amount, and instead stacks a $250 gross profit on a $1,300 carrier estimate to land a $1,550 customer rate, then works backward to a $1,350 ceiling for the truck [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:04:11]. Tony's Topics takes the subscription route, insisting lane rates need at least DAT One Pro at $135 a month, and shrugs that there is not much difference between 45 and 135 [wOpAqd5AALo @ 00:03:16]. Freight Broker 911 skips manual research altogether with an AI engine that returns instant quotes in about ten seconds off market data, lane history, fuel and capacity, at $0 for the first 30 days and $0 after that only with an active shipper moving at least one shipment every 30 days, otherwise $149 a month [edDHTJiH5HM @ 00:00:34].

The playbooks also diverge on who owns the customer and the carrier relationship. Mike Gray, appearing on Entre Mike, onboarded 14 direct shippers in a single year and kept only 2 or 3 of them, warning that direct shippers pay in 30 to 45 days and demand a system just to track invoices [oytUZVvyF80 @ 00:24:33]. FreightBrokers offers the agent route as the alternative to building all of that alone: a 60 percent split of a $300 margin leaves the agent $180, traded for the host brokerage's authority, systems, credit and carrier network, with a blunt instruction to read the agreement first [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:06:52]. Dispatchers split the room hardest. Gray says they bring negative sales skills and that a broker like Gray would pay a confident carrier two or three hundred dollars more, while the host adds a firsthand case of a dispatcher booking lower rates than the host's fiancé did and says dispatcher contact info in the packet adds friction [oytUZVvyF80 @ 00:10:19]. Yet the same conversation concedes that a carrier who lacks sales skills should hire a dispatcher anyway, with the host warning that the dispatcher then owns the broker relationship instead of the carrier [oytUZVvyF80 @ 00:31:06].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap every practitioner hits is confusing invoiced with paid. FreightBrokers walks a $2,100 shipper and $1,800 carrier load through POD-triggered invoicing, then shows that owing ten carriers means $18,000 out the door before a single shipper check lands, adding that a load can be profitable on paper and still create a cash flow problem [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:03:21]. That same $300 gross shrinks to $225 net once roughly $75 of load board, TMS, insurance, bond, phone, accounting and factoring expense comes off, which is why the channel defines net profit as what remains after the expenses of operating the business [Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:04:47]. BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS hits the carrier mirror image: fuel, insurance, drivers, truck payments and repairs do not wait for 30-, 45- or 60-day terms, and factoring will not fix low rates or high costs, since it may only help a carrier lose money more efficiently [ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:01:47]. Courtney at Bumble Bee Dispatch adds the friction cost of chasing pay without a single point of contact: five brokers in one week are hard to track, mailed checks can take two to three weeks, and truck stops charge to cash Comcheks [dTOcCujNdaw @ 00:05:00].

Pricing errors cut both ways. FreightBrokers opens with the stakes on a first load: quote too high and the first customer walks, quote too low and 500 bucks evaporates, which is why the channel derives a maximum carrier rate, $1,550 minus a $200 floor equals $1,350, and refuses to escalate until the profit disappears; if every carrier on the board wants $1,500, the move is to re-check the numbers or go back to the shipper [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:04:26]. When a competitor quotes $1,450, the instruction is to compare apples to apples and walk away if the margin does not work, because nobody needs to win every quote; the worked load still booked at $1,325 for $225 gross [HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:05:55]. ShipLeague warns new brokers off starting on a loss, contrasting $300 to $500 lost per load against $500 to $600 made at peaks, and says to quote very high or pass on year-round pricing and to ask for help before committing [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:11:45]. The same ShipLeague walkthrough flags a street-level abuse: do not post loads you do not have just to hear what carriers will haul for [rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:09:04].

The ugliest firsthand failure is fraud. Gray recounts a hotshot that deadheaded 400 miles near Billings, Montana for an 8:30 appointment and rolled in at 11:00, with the driver caught taping a handwritten paper sign over the truck's decal [oytUZVvyF80 @ 00:13:56]. The driver ran a new MC while the booked MC was 14 months old, the dispatcher could only get loads from TQL, and the fake trip lease meant the driver never got paid while every party, the broker included, carried fraud liability [oytUZVvyF80 @ 00:16:34]. On the factoring side, BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS lists the contract traps that eat the advance: ACH and wire fees, same-day funding charges, minimum volumes, processing and credit-check fees, reserves, early termination penalties, auto-renewal and aging fees, with tiered rates stepping up every 10, 15 or 30 days, so the carrier should demand a written total-cost example at 15, 30, 45 and 60 days [ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:03:36]. Non-recourse is narrower than it sounds, usually covering only insolvency and excluding disputes, missing POD, claims, rate-confirmation mismatches and refusals, so non-recourse does not necessarily mean a carrier can never be charged back [ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:03:00].

callout.title: Stop Before Booking, Signing or Scaling
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss, a fraud case or a cash crunch a practitioner reported firsthand. Clear all four before the next load moves.
items: Never book a carrier above your maximum carrier rate; if every carrier wants more, re-check the numbers or go back to the shipper [FreightBrokers — HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:04:26].

Search every caller's MC or DOT number for FMCSA authority, out-of-service status, safety rating and insurance, and pass on carriers with thin data [AscendTMS - The Free (and Best) TMS Software — ICIyOtMiEqY @ 00:15:42].
Never redirect payments after a notice of assignment, and know the scope of any UCC filing and how it gets released before signing [BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS — ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:05:26].
Fund the payables gap before adding loads: ten carriers at $1,800 is $18,000 out before a shipper pays [FreightBrokers — Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:03:21].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I read the spot and contract markets and know which lanes and load boards are paying right now?
chapters.title: Reading the Freight Market
chapters.subtitle: Spot vs. contract rates, tender rejection rates, weekly DAT hot-market and lane updates, diesel and truck-capacity shifts, and DAT vs. Truckstop by equipment type
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners reading the freight market run one loop: pull national averages, read tender rejections and load-to-truck ratios, then verify every hot map by searching real loads. Trucking Made Successful shows rejected contract freight hits the spot board in three to five days, so SONAR rejection maps work as a short-range rate forecast. Bobby Loads sets targets above DAT averages, at $3.40-$3.50 for dry van and $4-plus for flatbed, and chases $1,600-$2,000 days through short runs between hot markets like Chicago, Memphis, and the South, while dodging the West Coast and New England. Logistics Today reports 14% rejections and $6.35 diesel squeezing capacity. The splits come on contract versus spot, where Guy in a Truck weighs a $2.25 all-miles nursery contract against spot upside, and on DAT versus Truckstop, where operators disagree over analytics, specialized loads, and price.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who prices freight starts from the same split. Sarah at Anderson Trucking Service defines a contract rate as a fixed price and volume commitment on a set lane, usually for one year, a half year, or a quarter. It is built so a shipper can forecast spend and ride out swings. A spot rate is a one-time price that changes day to day and exists to find capacity for last-minute shipments across dry van, flatbed, and refrigerated [b2-QjzInPJo @ 00:00:21]. Miranda at Trucking Made Successful explains where contract rates come from: shippers run an annual RFP, and the winning bid becomes the rate. Those contracts are really not legally binding at all, which is why some people call them paper rates [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:01:41]. Dispatch Trucks adds the quoting difference operators trip over. Contract freight is priced as base plus fuel surcharge, while spot is quoted all-in, and contract terms generally favor shippers while spot favors carriers [5azQO8-P020 @ 00:08:40]. The shared takeaway is that the two prices run on different clocks. Contract rates lag by a few months, so carriers who locked reefer bids above $3 per mile in December 2021 out-earned spot carriers once 2022 crashed [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:03:09].

The second point of agreement is that tender rejections are the engine of the spot board. Miranda lays out the mechanism: when spot rates beat contract rates, carriers reject contract freight and that freight lands on the load board. That is why rejections fell sharply from late February 2022 and spot rates fell right along with them [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:04:06]. On the SONAR map, darker blue marks higher tender rejection and therefore higher spot rates. Elevation on the same map shows volume as tenders over the past seven days, so an operator reads height and color together. Because rejected freight reaches the spot market in three to five days, the map works as a short-range forecast [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:08:43]. Logistics Today reports the squeeze in its sharpest form: tender rejections around 14%, SONAR showing contract rates up 18%, new contracts up 12-13%, and backup carriers costing about 22% more. The outlet sums it up as contracts catching up [5cyp2cCCUiA @ 00:02:10]. It frames capacity as fewer trucks chasing more loads, with truck posts down 20-26% while van loads rose 17% [5cyp2cCCUiA @ 00:01:31]. The operator reading is simple: rising rejections mean contract freight is spilling into the spot pool, and the board will pay for it within days.

Every load-board practitioner also agrees that a colored map is a starting point, never a decision. Bobby Loads repeats it across episodes: don't just trust a red map, search the loads yourself [fzBhki-xaDc @ 00:13:38]. In another episode the line is that just because it's red does not mean it's hot [MDlMmII7ZrY @ 00:17:50]. In one update, Birmingham showed cool on the map while the actual loads were strong, including a $2,300 load at $6.61 per mile [2vUXF3RIbqg @ 00:04:02]. Bobby Loads also warns that load notes hide traps a map never shows: team loads, one-pick-three-drop runs, oversize loads, and $350K cargo. The geographic consensus is just as consistent. Bobby Loads calls the South money bags for flatbed and says to stay in hot areas. Miranda's regional breakdown independently ranks the South best for flatbed with about 49K loads and the West Coast worst, and puts the Midwest and South best for dry van with the West and Northeast worst [l6yFrAoUZ2M @ 00:03:13]. Both camps steer away from the Northeast and the West Coast. Both treat load boards the way Bobby Loads puts it: as tools, not money printers. The operator who wins checks the map, opens the actual postings, reads the notes, and only then books.
