sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Bobby Loads opens every update the same way: pull DAT national averages, then set a target well above them. In one week dry van sat at $3.03, flatbed at $3.66, and reefer at $3.44, with diesel at $5.31. The targets were 3.40-3.50 for vans and about $4 for flatbed [Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:00:23]. Another week put dry van at $3.08, flatbed at $3.77, and reefer at $3.44, with targets of $3.40-$3.50, $4-plus, and $3.60-$3.80 respectively [MDlMmII7ZrY @ 00:00:11]. On a Sunday, the read uses the previous 8 days of data. When the market softened to $2.72 van, $3.44 flatbed, and $3.19 reefer, the van target dropped to $3.00-$3.20 [ZSqNEq3Cx_g @ 00:00:34]. The heuristic for raw load-to-truck counts is to cut the loads in half and double or triple the truck count. A market only counts as tight if it still looks tight after that haircut [Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:03:56]. Memphis cleared that bar at 3,752 loads against 405 trucks. Chicago ran about 6,000 loads to 1,000 trucks, and Indianapolis showed 5,000-plus loads against fewer than 500 trucks.

The unit economics are built per day, not per mile alone. The dry van daily target is $1,600-$2,000 or more. It is earned by running short hops between good markets instead of big miles into crappy areas, with sample hits like Decatur to Indy at $1,900 and $4.75 per mile [2vUXF3RIbqg @ 00:05:20]. Flatbed runs on a weekly rhythm: short runs during the week, then a gross pad load for the weekend, aiming for close to $10K per week. The same plan consolidates LTL out of Chicago and avoids Northwest Arkansas [Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:14:20]. The flatbed playbook stays South and Midwest, uses 800-1,200-mile Friday runs east, and then eats one on Monday. Bobby Loads' own drivers posted $12,120 on 2,773 miles at $4.37 and $13,700 on 3,099 miles at $4.42 [2vUXF3RIbqg @ 00:10:14]. Jonesboro, Arkansas flatbed freight paid $3,200 for 395 miles and $4,600 for 640 miles. Other specific loads show what the targets look like in practice: Montgomery to Gainesville at $7 per mile, an 822-mile run paying $4,450 for roughly $2,200 a day, Memphis to Dallas at $6,000 on 452 miles, and Shreveport to Oklahoma City at $9.90 per mile [MDlMmII7ZrY @ 00:11:55]. The rule underneath it all: the less you drive and the better the RPM, the better the profit.

The tool stack splits by job. Bobby Loads rates DAT best for dry van, reefer, flatbed, stepdeck, and Conestoga on volume and analytics, with a map similar to SONAR. Truckstop has the edge for double drops and RGNs but otherwise carries the same loads with weaker analytics [s-t9YGcOJ8U @ 00:00:37]. Contract Fortune calls DAT the McDonald's of posting. They prefer Truckstop's rate calculator, which lands within a couple hundred dollars, plus its national fuel averages. They recommend holding both memberships, noting DAT services ran about $300 against about $100 at Truckstop [ocF4fny2uH8 @ 00:08:23]. Trucking Made Successful runs the SONAR app plus Truckstop/FTR Intel because the daily register stopped showing new authorities [M0KZ3BZctSQ @ 00:00:15]. Bobby Loads pushes the DAT market-conditions package, priced at about $100 extra a month and pitched as worth 100 bucks on a single load. They pair it with DAT trend lines and RateView [ZSqNEq3Cx_g @ 00:00:10]. Load Hunter, a sponsored add-on, layers factoring credit scores, click-to-email and click-to-call templates, lane auto-email, a profit calculator, and broker reviews on top of the boards. Contract Fortune adds the clock on the broker side: brokers have 24-36 hours to cover freight, and that is the window a carrier negotiates inside.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to lock freight or chase the board. Sarah at Anderson Trucking Service sells contract as the shipper's safety play: a fixed price and volume commitment on a set lane, usually for a year, with predictable costs, negotiable fuel and accessorials, less admin time and capacity on each and every load [b2-QjzInPJo @ 00:01:05]. Dispatch Trucks flips the lens to the carrier side, arguing contract rates usually favor shippers while spot rates favor carriers, and that contract pays base plus fuel surcharge while spot is quoted all-in [5azQO8-P020 @ 00:08:40]. Miranda at Trucking Made Successful undercuts the whole idea of a lock, calling contracts really not legally binding at all, so-called paper rates. Yet the same breakdown shows contract carriers who bid reefer above $3 a mile in December 2021 out-earning spot carriers after the 2022 crash, because contract rates lag by a few months [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:03:09]. Guy in a Truck weighs a live offer: a floral nursery contract at $2.25 a mile plus $50 per stop, five to six stops on regional runs, grossing five to six grand a week with home time. They frame it as good stability versus the spot market, with the risk of losing out if in-season spot rates climb [6qAGWwbnmxA @ 00:04:02].

Which screen to trust is the second fault line. Bobby Loads rates DAT best for dry van, reefer, flatbed, stepdeck and Conestoga on volume and analytics and calls its map similar to SONAR. Truckstop gets the edge only for double drops and RGNs; otherwise it carries the same loads with weaker analytics [s-t9YGcOJ8U @ 00:00:37]. Contract Fortune splits the job differently: DAT is the place to post, like McDonald's, while Truckstop wins on a rate calculator accurate within a couple hundred dollars and on its national fuel averages. DAT services ran about $300 against roughly $100 at Truckstop, and the recommendation is to hold both memberships [ocF4fny2uH8 @ 00:00:51]. Trucking Made Successful skips the board debate for forecasting and pays for FreightWaves SONAR, because the data they needed was locked behind SONAR or ACT Research [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:00:14]. Later they layered the SONAR app with Truckstop and FTR Intel after the daily register stopped showing new authorities [M0KZ3BZctSQ @ 00:00:15]. The practical read: Bobby Loads runs one platform plus the paid market-conditions package, Contract Fortune runs two boards for posting versus pricing, and Miranda treats tender-rejection data as the leading indicator that board volume only confirms three to five days later.

Relationships and lane discipline split the field a third way. Bobby Loads plays pure geography: short runs bouncing between good markets beat stacking big miles into crappy areas. The daily target is $1,600 to $2,000 or more, with a standing refusal to run cheap inbound loads to California [2vUXF3RIbqg @ 00:04:45]. Dispatch Trucks pushes a blended book instead, rejecting the rates-are-crap, go-direct-to-shippers mindset and teaching six practices: assess risk tolerance, match operational capacity, analyze the market, diversify with contracts covering baseline costs and spot capturing peaks, build relationships, and review regularly [5azQO8-P020 @ 00:07:52]. On broker loyalty, Guy in a Truck invests deliberately. When a broker has $3,300 into a load and offers a $3,350 ceiling, they take $3,300 to build the relationship, figuring brokers make maybe a hundred bucks if they're lucky [6qAGWwbnmxA @ 00:12:59]. Miranda at Trucking Made Successful is colder, warning that relationships built during COVID didn't really mean anything and sticking to known, smaller brokers. They also insist posted rates are pre-negotiation and that the rates you can negotiate are going to make diesel not an issue [l6yFrAoUZ2M @ 00:05:22]. One camp spends margin to buy loyalty; the other treats every rate confirmation as a fresh fight.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated trap is trusting the map instead of the loads. Bobby Loads warns that red on the flatbed map can be a false positive and that just cuz it's red does not mean it's hot, pushing operators to search the delivery market a day or two ahead [MDlMmII7ZrY @ 00:09:25]. The same warning lands in the 2026 lane breakdown: don't just trust a red map, search the loads yourself [fzBhki-xaDc @ 00:13:38]. The reverse error costs money too. Birmingham showed cool on the dry van map while the actual loads were strong, including a $2,300 run at $6.61 a mile [2vUXF3RIbqg @ 00:04:02]. On the West Coast, the numbers themselves are suspect: Bobby Loads says brokers repost the same flatbed loads, and the standing rule is I would always stay away from the West Coast, I don't trust these numbers [C4qKjPG0gcY @ 00:01:26]. Indy loads hide extra stops in the notes, so the rate per mile on screen is not the job actually being booked. Gross is the final illusion: in New England and on the West Coast, Bobby Loads repeats that gross does not mean anything, and flatbed operators are told to avoid bad areas that force layovers no matter what the posted number shows.

Broker-side traps show up as both fraud and friction. Bobby Loads flags a Kahaba load listing a Gmail contact, which they allegedly tie to a hacked account. The rule that follows is blunt: distrust rates far above market, so don't fall for this crap, please [ZSqNEq3Cx_g @ 00:05:56]. Contract Fortune exposes the margin squeeze on Florida outbound, which is cheap to begin with. On a load paying $1,100 to $1,200, the broker paid the driver $500 to $600, against a normal broker target of $200 to $300 per load [ocF4fny2uH8 @ 00:02:27]. Miranda at Trucking Made Successful reports that brokers are pleasant to work with but hold carriers verbally, including holding a truck about two hours waiting on a rate confirmation. They add that it has been a nightmare until just recently, which leaves them suspicious after the 2022 downturn [M0KZ3BZctSQ @ 00:11:26]. Shippers face their own reversal: at renewal time, contract carriers may also leave the market. A contract that looked locked can vanish when spot beats it and rejected tenders send the freight back to the load board [ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:07:32]. These traps all punish the operator who books the headline number without checking the contact, the margin and the commitment.

The economics check that sinks carriers is diesel hiding inside the all-in rate. Logistics Today puts the DAT all-in van rate at $3.07 but only $2.24 excluding fuel, and says that 80-plus cent gap is mostly diesel, with diesel at $6.35 and roughly $2.50 above the prior year [5cyp2cCCUiA @ 00:01:10]. Bobby Loads quantifies the hit at the truck level: diesel at $5.64, up 4.44 percent, with fuel running $2,000 to $3,000 a week. The counter is to cite diesel prices directly when negotiating with brokers [ZSqNEq3Cx_g @ 00:12:11]. Contract Fortune cuts the bill at the pump, partial-filling about $150 in pricey states, filling up where fuel is cheaper and avoiding the mountains [ocF4fny2uH8 @ 00:04:37]. The mileage trap compounds it. Bobby Loads rejects LA to Houston at about $2.81 because it is not worth 1,500 miles, and sums the rule up elsewhere as less you drive, better RPM, the better profit's going to be [Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:15:38]. Run the check before booking: strip fuel out of the posted number, compare the linehaul to what the week actually costs, and refuse long cheap runs into areas that force layovers.

chapters.question_prompt: How do dry van, reefer, flatbed, oversize, and drayage/intermodal freight differ, and how do I source loads in each?
chapters.title: Equipment Niches: Van, Reefer, Flatbed, Heavy Haul and Drayage
chapters.subtitle: Reefer basics for new brokers, booking differences by trailer type, oversize/heavy-haul pay, container drayage from port pickup to empty return, intermodal lane bidding, and load-board search walkthroughs
chapters.executive_summary: Operators working van, reefer, flatbed, heavy haul and drayage agree that dry van is the weakest seat and that margin sits in equipment and paperwork most operators avoid. Chief Carriers reports a 15-truck heavy-haul carrier near $8 million in revenue, almost double a regular flatbed operation. Reefer and flatbed are priced like van but booked off tighter checklists covering commodity, temperature, dimensions and securement. Load-board operators grade posts on true rate over all miles, deadhead and broker pay history, with Cole Fairbrook calling $2.35 a mile a loss. Drayage runs on SCAC, UIIA, TWIC, last free dates and empty returns, and one live intermodal bid landed at $1,450 on 600 round-trip miles plus accessorials. Disagreements cover what a SCAC costs and whether brokers strictly need one, LoadMatch's value, and whether to bid high or anchor to recent runs.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the van, reefer, flatbed and specialized desks, the practitioners converge on one point: plain dry van is the weakest place to stand, and margin lives in equipment that fewer operators can run. Chief Carriers opens with 'the riches are in the niches' and reports oversized and heavy haul thriving while van, reefer and flatbed sit flat, with infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture and construction driving demand [7kg1eMOTev8 @ 00:00:13]. Few equipped carriers translate into pricing power, and the work is often project-based one-offs with no standard price. AFT Dispatch puts numbers on the van weakness: van rejection ran just over 3% amid overcapacity, the lowest performer since May 2023, while flatbed averaged over 10% rejection in 2023 and hit 20% three times, and reefer ran 6% with holiday peaks [Gx_gladG4ps @ 00:06:00]. Bobby Loads' caller, running three trucks split across flatbed, reefer and van, says the move if starting over would be to avoid dry van entirely [jxL6kaRxoEo @ 00:00:00]. The same view surfaces on the load-board side: Cole Fairbrook quotes DAT per-mile averages without fuel surcharge at flatbed 279, reefer 264 and dry van 228, so van sits at the bottom of the national rate stack before a single phone call is made [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:02:24].

The second consensus point is that each trailer type is sold with the same pricing logic but booked with a different checklist. Brandon Scott, who started in reefer with no experience, says reefer is priced the same way as van or flatbed, reefer fuel does not need to be factored precisely, and the marketplace 'will correct your price' once the number goes out [xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:03:33]. No dedicated reefer network is required; good-paying freight posted on a load board draws carriers, though scarce lanes may get no calls, and the driver sets and maintains the unit while the broker only supplies the temperature [xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:05:05]. Never Stop Trucking turns that into a booking discipline. On flatbed, confirm trailer length, spread-axle weight distribution, length, width, height and state-by-state overhang rules, with roughly 13 feet 5 inches to 13 feet 6 inches as the ceiling including deck height, plus straps, chains and tarps [K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:00:45]. On reefer, confirm the exact commodity, because some drivers refuse meat, fish or watermelons, along with temperature, pre-cool, continuous mode, air chute and e-tracks, and expect long dwell, overnight appointments and multi-stop runs in exchange for higher pay [K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:06:20]. Dry van still needs weight, pallet count and packaging confirmed, with straps on board [K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:10:41].

Drayage is where every speaker agrees the paperwork is the moat. FreightBrokers defines it as moving 10, 20 or 40-foot containers to or from a port or rail terminal and lists the baseline: a SCAC code from nmfta.org for both brokers and carriers at about $80, the UIIA agreement for carriers but not brokers, a TWIC card for port drivers, and fees on any delay in pickup, delivery or container return that truckload never charges [N1uEW-kxNvE @ 00:02:16]. Freightskills confirms brokers technically need no license to contract a dray carrier, still recommends the four-letter NMFTA SCAC at about $70, and stresses that UIIA is port-specific with no reciprocity, so a carrier approved for the California ports might not be able to go to Chicago, and New Jersey works the same way [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:10:07]. CONGO EXPRESS gives the carrier-side build order: authority, UIIA-friendly insurance, SCAC, UIIA, then LoadMatch [vSgjLSdmTKc @ 00:07:31]. Drayage Specialist frames why the niche matters: dray is the short-distance link between ships or rail and warehouses, it prevents port bottlenecks and supports just-in-time delivery, and specialist carriers who know port operations and permits are the ones who get it done [sv8u2e9X6Oc @ 00:01:16]. Freightskills adds that every truckload customer has drayage at some point, which makes it an upsell on existing accounts [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:03:09].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the load boards, the mechanics are arithmetic plus speed. Real Trucking Money runs both DAT and Truckstop because good loads book in minutes, searches a 100-mile radius by equipment, and grades every post on three numbers: true rate, meaning total pay over all miles including deadhead, the deadhead itself, and broker pay history, where 3 days at $2.80 beats 45 days at $3.10 [Xi2gMYEX18k @ 00:04:39]. Dispatch Desk USA shows the math: $1,600 for 400 loaded miles is $4 a mile, but adding 100 deadhead miles drops it to $3.20 per all miles, which then gets compared against a cost-plus-profit floor [w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:04:29]. Cole Fairbrook sets the floor bluntly: $2.35 a mile is 'pretty much a loss,' a truck 'really got to be over the 250 mark,' 263 is barely above break-even, and a Tampa load at 1.88 means 'paying the broker' [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:20:05]. Fairbrook filters Truckstop at a $3 minimum and a 250 to 500-mile length of haul, prices deadhead into the counter, and uses the paid Load Hunter Chrome extension, whose RPM Plus folds deadhead in and turned a 394 post into 376 [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:13:40]. Dispatch Desk USA adds that DAT wins on van and reefer volume while Truckstop is stronger in flatbed and open deck, so the trailer type decides which board gets checked first [w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:01:31].

Dispatching & Intermodal Training bid a Houston port to Wylie, Texas lane live, and the sequence is replicable. Mileage comes from Google Maps by zip code, with a check on whether the carrier has an EZ tag for tolls; the 299-mile estimate rounds to 300, and because dray miles are doubled for the round trip, the quote is built on 600 miles with no backhaul needed [SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:03:31]. No target rate came with the request, so new dispatchers should ask the broker for one. Market sat near $2.80 a mile, carriers want about $3, which is 'hard to get,' and the stated rule is to bid high because the broker will negotiate down. Yet 600 times 2.80 produced $1,680 linehaul, which the speaker judged too high and likely to be overlooked [SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:05:40]. The final bid was $1,450, anchored to a nearby Grapevine run at about $1,400 less than two weeks earlier [SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:06:30]. Accessorials then go on top: chassis at about $25 a day doubled to $50, storage at truck-parking rate times two for $50, an overweight fee even on a declared-legal load, $125 pre-pull, and $60 an hour detention after 2 hours [SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:08:00]. Freightskills explains why those lines matter: carriers borrow the chassis and box from the steamship line and port, carry the fee liability, and pass it to the broker [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:08:43].

For import boxes, Drayage Academy lays out a 12-step workflow that starts with the delivery order, covering number, container, steamship line, weight, size, type, terminal and delivery location, then holds, fees and gate PIN, then confirming that customs, the steamship line and the terminal have all released the box [fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:01:54]. The last free date is the hinge, because the carrier is liable if it misses an agreed pickup: 'So don't miss your LFD' [fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:04:54]. The back half covers chassis inspection and the EIR, container and seal verification, the out-gate EIR, logged appointment times for detention, the signed delivery order, the empty-return location from the steamship line, and the in-gate EIR proving the empty was accepted [fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:08:18]. On exports, Victor Mason reads the booking as 'a reservation of space' on a specific vessel, identifies lines by prefix, CMAU for CMA, 038BM for MSC and ONEYU for ONE, and tracks ERD as the opening of the receiving window, cargo cutoff as the last receiving day, and doc cutoff as the customs deadline [o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 00:12:10]. Mason's prospecting method is to drive a 3 to 5-mile radius around the port listing businesses with containers parked outside, while Freightskills uses Import Yeti as a free lead source that likely needs no account [o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 00:33:03] [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:05:11].

callout.title: Desk-Level Edges From The Load Boards And The Port
callout.body: Small moves the practitioners use to find, price and pitch niche freight faster than the next desk.
items: Call the newest postings first, and read the posting comments, which hide costs such as tarps, lumpers and appointments [Dispatch Desk USA — w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:03:35].

Let the broker quote first, ask for $3.10, then go quiet: 'Silence is your friend on the phone,' and sometimes 10% is sitting there that was not offered up front [Real Trucking Money — Xi2gMYEX18k @ 00:06:28].

53-foot trailers are scarce, so brokers raise rates to cover them, while 48-foot trailers are more versatile; on short hauls cut the deadhead filter to 75 miles [Cole Fairbrook — bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:28:15].
On drayage sales calls, say you have 'capacity,' never 'empties' [Victor Mason — o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 01:14:06].

sop_steps.title: Pull the free market read
sop_steps.action: Check the weekly national report and state-level loads in versus loads out before choosing lanes.
sop_steps.detail: Use dat.com, Resources, Blogs for the free weekly report and the Dean Croke video, then read the DAT state dashboard, where Alabama showed 392 loads in against 2,063 out and Texas had fewer than half of 3,500 deliveries reloading [Cole Fairbrook — bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:00:49].

sop_steps.title: Screen both boards every morning
sop_steps.action: Spend 15 minutes on DAT and 15 on Truckstop with tight filters on radius, equipment and pickup date.
sop_steps.detail: A good load is posted within the hour, above the lane average, with a reasonable window and short deadhead; a $1.80 post on a $2.50-average lane or a post sitting 6 hours unbooked is a red flag [Real Trucking Money — Xi2gMYEX18k @ 00:03:09].

sop_steps.title: Price on all miles and verify the broker
sop_steps.action: Convert every offer to rate per all miles, check pay history and authority, and lock the rate in writing.
sop_steps.detail: Verify MC authority on FMCSA SAFER even for Book It Now loads, get the rate confirmation in writing, and treat rates far above market, vague postings and bad factorability as red flags [Dispatch Desk USA — w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:05:31].

sop_steps.title: Quote and run the dray move
sop_steps.action: Build the round-trip linehaul, stack accessorials, then manage LFD, EIRs and the empty return.
sop_steps.detail: Anchor linehaul to recent nearby runs, as with the $1,450 Wylie bid [Dispatching & Intermodal Training — SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:06:30], then confirm the LFD and get the empty-return location from the steamship line, because the empty does not always go back to the terminal where it was picked up [Drayage Academy — fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:08:18].

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over whether dry van is worth running at all. Bobby Loads, fielding a caller with three trucks spread across flatbed, reefer and van, says that if starting over they would stay away from dry van [jxL6kaRxoEo @ 00:00:00]. Yet the same channel reports its own van averaging 240 a mile, up from 210, and credits non-domiciled drivers leaving the market for the bump [jxL6kaRxoEo @ 00:04:54]. AFT Dispatch frames van as the weakest segment on paper: tender rejection just over 3%, overcapacity, and the lowest performer since May 2023 [Gx_gladG4ps @ 00:06:00]. AFT then shows a van booking for Reggie at 545 a mile on short runs and 402 on the week, so a sharp desk can still beat a soft segment, a point Thomas sums up as 'all an averages game.' Brandon Scott pushes back on the idea that reefer is a separate science: reefer gets priced exactly the way van or flatbed does, reefer fuel does not need precise math, and the broker should take a number to the marketplace, which 'will correct your price' [xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:03:33]. For an operator, segment averages set the backdrop, but lane selection and booking discipline decide whether a given equipment type pays.

How much a broker must know about the reefer box itself is where Brandon Scott and Never Stop Trucking split hardest. Brandon Scott, whose first freight was reefer with no prior experience, says no dedicated reefer network is needed: post good-paying freight on a load board, and the driver sets and maintains the unit while the broker only supplies the temperature [xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:05:05]. Ennis at Never Stop Trucking runs a far heavier checklist: confirm the exact commodity because some drivers refuse meat, fish or watermelons, then confirm temperature, pre-cool, continuous run, air chute and e-tracks, and expect long dwell times, overnight appointments and multi-stop runs in exchange for higher pay [K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:06:20]. Ennis also warns that temperature trackers can produce a rejected load and an insurance claim. On damage, Brandon Scott argues reefer carries no special curse: most damage comes from forklifts during loading and unloading, a shipper may simply write off damaged boxes, and risk follows the commodity, such as potatoes, rather than the trailer type [xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:02:01]. Bobby Loads adds a seasonal twist that blurs the line entirely: Christmas-tree freight that ships dry flips to reefer once freezes hit, so the equipment a lane demands can change in the middle of a season [jxL6kaRxoEo @ 00:02:04].

Drayage practitioners split on paperwork, carrier sourcing and pricing posture. FreightBrokers tells brokers and carriers alike to get a SCAC code through nmfta.org for about an $80 fee [N1uEW-kxNvE @ 00:02:16], while Freightskills states that brokers technically need no license to contract a drayage carrier, yet still recommends the four-letter NMFTA SCAC at about $70 [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:07:47]. On sourcing, CONGO EXPRESS calls loadmatch.com 'the best kept secret,' reports 200 to 300 broker emails after posting truck capacity, and pays about $600 a year or about $150 per three months [vSgjLSdmTKc @ 00:00:30]. Freightskills, claiming no affiliation, calls the same site dated, noting carrier names are free while contacts sit behind a paid tier. Pricing posture diverges too. Dispatching & Intermodal Training says carriers want about $3 a mile, which is 'hard to get,' and advises bidding high because the broker will negotiate down. Yet on a Houston-port-to-Wylie lane, the speaker pulled 299 miles from Google Maps by zip code, rounded to 300, doubled it to 600 for the round trip, priced it at $2.80 for $1,680, judged that too high for the broker to take seriously, and bid $1,450 off a nearby Grapevine run near $1,400 [SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:06:30].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Load-board traps hit operators who read posted numbers at face value. Cole Fairbrook warns that brokers double- and triple-post loads, inflating apparent volume [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:03:05], spots a $15,000 post for 472 miles that is probably a typo for $1,500, and sets hard floors: $2.35 a mile is 'pretty much a loss,' the target has to be over the 250 mark, and Tampa at 1.88 means 'paying the broker' [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:20:05]. Real Trucking Money flags a $1.80 post on a $2.50-average lane as a cheap-broker signal, treats $1,200 for 700 miles as under $2 a mile, and says a post sitting six hours unbooked should raise questions [Xi2gMYEX18k @ 00:02:31]. The same channel ranks pay history over headline rate: three days to pay at $2.80 beats 45 days at $3.10, because 'cash flow keeps your truck moving.' Dispatch Desk USA warns that posting comments hide tarps, lumpers and appointments, that 'a posting you cannot run is not a load,' and that even Book It Now loads need an MC authority check on FMCSA SAFER first, plus a written rate confirmation and a hard rule to never pay anyone to book a load [w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:03:35].

Drayage failures are measured in fees that do not exist in truckload. FreightBrokers lists delays at pickup, delivery or container return as the core cost difference from truckload freight [N1uEW-kxNvE @ 00:05:48]. Victor Mason describes a Los Angeles carrier ingating a container on the wrong booking; a dray out runs $500 to $4,000 and up to about $5,000, and because that box sat on top it cost about $700, which Mason deducted from the carrier's invoice [o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 00:07:39]. On CMA reefer boxes in NY/NJ, Mason quotes 3 free days, then $690 a day, then $895, then $1,040, reaching about $13,000 over 14 days, and recalls a customer paying about $30k a month in demurrage who shut that division down. Keisha at Drayage Academy opens with the three classic losses, false port trips, unpaid demurrage and returns to the wrong location, then hammers two rules: 'don't miss your LFD,' since the carrier is liable for a missed agreed pickup, and 'do not assume the empty container goes back to the same terminal where you picked it up' [fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:08:18]. Freightskills adds that holding a UIIA 'is not the only part,' and brokers who skip due diligence put themselves in danger [o6WTbGsyLqg @ 00:06:13].

Lane and equipment traps punish operators who chase headline rates. Cole Fairbrook's West Coast check found Ogden to Seattle posted at $2,000 against a $2,400 average with only seven loads, and a Portland-to-Denver round trip near $8,500 whose return option was a single load from an unapproved broker [bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:42:32]; the same speaker warns that van freight hides catches like round trips, 17 drops and 48-hour drop trailers. Bobby Loads avoids California unless the load is something like 3,000 miles for $11K, calling it saturated with undercutting, and notes Southeast flatbed rates stay low because brokers price in the Florida-to-Georgia deadhead [jxL6kaRxoEo @ 00:03:43]. On open deck, Ennis at Never Stop Trucking warns that flatbed loads need frequent securement checks because falling cargo 'can kill someone' [K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:10:23]. Andrew Winkler at Chief Carriers lists the heavy-haul bottlenecks: pilot cars, routing, limited operating hours and no moving after dark, and relays that the hardest move the featured owner faced was not a heavy piece but a delicate fiberglass or carbon-fiber load on a stretch trailer [7kg1eMOTev8 @ 00:04:02]. That owner reached 15 trucks and about $8 million in revenue, which Winkler calls almost double what a regular flatbed carrier does.

chapters.question_prompt: How should I handle detention, layover, TONU and other accessorial charges without losing carriers or margin?
chapters.title: Accessorials: Detention, Layover and TONU
chapters.subtitle: Definitions and differences, carrier tactics for getting paid, broker obligations and policies, rate disputes, dispatcher responsibility, and how brokers profit from or lose on accessorials
chapters.executive_summary: Carriers, dispatchers and brokers converge on one rule: if detention, layover and TONU terms are not in the rate confirmation or broker-carrier agreement before the truck rolls, the money is mostly gone. The street baseline is two free hours, then roughly $30-$75 per hour, with $50 cited most often by brokers. TONU clusters at $150-$200, and layover runs anywhere from $100 per night to $500 or more. Collection is a documentation game: timestamped arrival emails, warnings before free time expires, in/out times on the bill of lading, and invoices chased until paid. The fights are over who eats the cost when the shipper refuses. Some brokers pay from their own pocket, others pay only what the customer approves. The other split is whether brokers should pass accessorials through at cost or mark them up for margin.

key_metrics.label: Industry-Standard Detention Policy
key_metrics.context: A broker's stated view of the typical, fair detention policy that brokers should adopt and carriers should demand on the rate con

key_metrics.label: Published Detention Rate Band
key_metrics.context: Standard hourly detention band, paid in half-hour or hourly increments after two free hours

key_metrics.label: Common-Practice TONU
key_metrics.context: Typical truck-order-not-used payment regardless of whether the driver deadheaded two miles or 200 miles to the pickup

key_metrics.label: Negotiated TONU Win
key_metrics.context: TONU a dispatcher collected after flagging cancellation risk when the broker moved the pickup, versus the $150 default offer

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every seat in the deal agrees on is two hours of unpaid dock time, then the meter starts. Nate Cross of Freight 360 calls it free time, pegs the industry standard at two hours, and says roughly $50 an hour is normal once a driver passes it [A7rlv69JAj8 @ 00:01:59]. Think Trucking quotes the same two free hours and a wider $30 to $75 hourly band, paid in half-hour or hourly increments [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:00:52]. Ernest at Never Stop Trucking spells out the math that burns rookies: if a truck sits four hours under a two-hour policy, only the last two get paid, at anywhere from $25 to $50 an hour. Ernest treats $50 as the bare minimum because the broker is renting a running truck, its fuel, and a driver, not an hourly factory worker [tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:03:18]. Everybody scraps over this money because of opportunity cost. Trucking Territory puts a one-load-a-day driver at $800 to $1,200 in daily revenue. A six-hour hold erases time that could have been spent driving and earning. Dispatchers only get paid when the driver gets paid, so they hate detention as much as drivers do [Q-HgB9nn1jI @ 00:00:22].

Second point of near-total agreement: if the terms are not written down before the truck is dispatched, they effectively do not exist. Think Trucking puts it as the rule that if it is not in the rate confirmation, it does not exist. Accessorial pay only becomes real when it is written before the work happens [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:03:40]. The ShipLeague broker is stunned by how rarely dispatchers or drivers ask about detention. They grill a broker on commodity, weight, distance and rate, but skip detention. ShipLeague demands the amount and start time in black and white on the rate con, noting it takes no time at all because the driver is the one who will actually sit there [OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:00:18]. Tim at Freight Master Resources walked a carrier friend through exactly that failure. The appointment was noon, the driver was on site at 10:30, and the real appointment turned out to be 6 a.m. the next day. Nothing about detention or layover was in either the rate confirmation or the carrier setup packet, so the broker threw roughly $150 and walked [1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:03:31]. Brandon Scott assigns the responsibility bluntly from the brokerage chair: the carrier has to make sure the broker has a detention policy in place. Without one, there is a very real possibility of collecting nothing [V11p0IBJsTk @ 00:04:21].

The third consensus: the carrier bills the broker, and paper beats phone calls. Pauline Nabacwa, speaking as a dispatcher and company owner, is explicit that the broker pays detention. The broker may later chase the shipper for it, but the carrier side bills the broker directly [fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:06:03]. Brandon Scott explains the plumbing: the shipper's relationship is with the broker, not the carrier, so the detention policy that governs is the broker's. The broker's job is to negotiate a policy with the shipper up front so the carrier can be paid when hours stretch [V11p0IBJsTk @ 00:03:41]. Craig Bliss has worked the shipper, broker and carrier sides. Craig says verbal conversations do not prove detention, especially against brokers that go quiet once the request lands; the paper trail does. Any phone call gets recapped in the same email chain with a 'per our conversation' line [WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:04:53]. Yvonne of Freightbrokerchic runs the identical playbook toward the customer. The moment an on-time driver is being held, the shipper is notified and the driver is told to keep track of time. Every phone call is followed up by email, so nobody can later claim they did not know a detention was coming [zvX7UreND4E @ 00:09:20].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The street rate card is wide, and practitioners quote it to the dollar. The spread between low and high offers is where negotiation lives. Trucking Territory works with $30 for each extra hour past two, and $100 to $150 per night of layover when the broker is reasonable [Q-HgB9nn1jI @ 00:03:17]. Pauline Nabacwa reports the floor going lower: brokers offering $12, $15 or $20 an hour, or a flat $100, $150 or $200 for the whole wait. Pauline calls that cheap change against what the truck gives up [fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:03:41]. Ernest at Never Stop Trucking adds the cap buried in many policies: a typical broker policy pays $50 an hour up to a $250 maximum, then flips to layover. Layover commonly lands at $200 to $250 a day, roughly $10 to $12 an hour once divided by 24. TONU is a flat $150 whether the driver deadheaded two miles or 200 [tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:05:33]. Nate Cross at Freight 360 prices layover higher on the broker side, at around $500 depending on equipment. Nate sets TONU near $200 and extra stops at $50 to $100 each. Lumpers run roughly $75 up to $200, reimbursed against a receipt or advanced to the driver up front [A7rlv69JAj8 @ 00:05:06].

Collection runs on a timed email sequence, and Craig Bliss hands it out nearly word for word. On arrival, the carrier emails the broker something like: driver has arrived at the shipper as of 1300, detention will start at 1500 at $50 per hour, and a heads-up will follow before it starts [WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:02:33]. At about 90 minutes, a second email in the same chain notes the driver is still not loaded at 1430 and offers to help speed loading. At expiry, a third email says detention is now running. After loading, a final email carries total charges plus the bill of lading with in and out times. Think Trucking runs the same five-step drill. First, the clause goes on the rate con. Second, the carrier sends a timestamped written arrival notice rather than a phone call. Third comes a warning before free time ends. Fourth, in and out times go on the BOL, initialed by facility staff, with gate tickets and photos kept. Fifth, the invoice is chased until it lands on settlement [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:07:00]. Trucking Territory adds a field tactic: the two-hour call itself can push the broker to get the truck loaded faster to save money. If the next pickup is at risk, call that broker too and try to move the appointment to the next day [Q-HgB9nn1jI @ 00:04:47].

On the broker side, the mechanics turn on approval paperwork and, for some, margin. Brandon Scott emails the shipper the situation and the PO number, then gets the PO approved for detention. Brandon then issues the carrier a new rate confirmation showing the accumulated detention hours, so the final invoice includes it [V11p0IBJsTk @ 00:08:16]. Freight 360 does the same on TONU. The broker confirms what the customer typically pays on cancellation and invoices the customer the $200. The broker then cuts a fresh rate con to the driver for $200 and makes zero margin on the transaction [7sfi19fbIzU @ 00:02:52]. Brandon Manney teaches the opposite money play: ask every shipper its detention and layover rates during the sale, then pay the carrier less than collected. In Manney's example, a shipper pays $200 an hour for two hours, $400 total. The broker pays the carrier $100 an hour and keeps $200, or collects $500 on a layover and pays $400 or $300 [8Mhf3iqBflw @ 00:04:09]. Carriers can flip the paperwork too. Tim at Freight Master Resources has carriers draft their own detention and layover terms as a PDF and send them for signature through DocuSign or similar. That lets them negotiate from $75 an hour down to $40 or $50 instead of accepting $20 to $25 after three or four hours [1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:07:39].

callout.title: Collection Edges Practitioners Actually Use
callout.body: Small timing and paperwork moves that separate paid accessorial claims from ignored ones.
items: If the broker moves the appointment after the truck is already committed, anchor detention to the original rate-con time. On an 8 a.m. appointment with two free hours, the hosts would pay 10 to 1, three hours of detention [Freight 360 — xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:09:16]

Raise TONU the moment detention starts building or the broker shifts the pickup. Pauline Nabacwa turned a $150 default into $540 by flagging the cancellation risk early, partly through pity and partly through negotiation [Pauline Nabacwa — fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:10:53]
The two-hour grace period is measured from appointment time, not arrival. Showing up early and sitting an hour before the appointment may not count at all [Think Trucking — uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:01:10]
If the broker goes silent, keep the same email chain and add the broker's accounting team and other operational staff to it [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:04:36]

sop_steps.title: Lock Terms at Booking
sop_steps.action: Ask the broker about the detention rate per hour, when detention starts, and the layover and TONU terms, then get them all written on the rate con.
sop_steps.detail: Ask before booking whether the broker pays detention, at what hourly rate, and after how many hours. If they refuse, do not stack a tight reload behind that load, and try negotiating a better line rate [Trucking Territory — Q-HgB9nn1jI @ 00:04:12]

sop_steps.title: Timestamp Arrival in Writing
sop_steps.action: Email the broker the moment the driver checks in, stating the arrival time, the detention start time and the hourly rate.
sop_steps.detail: Use a script like: driver arrived at the shipper as of 1300, detention will start at 1500 at $50 per hour, and a heads-up will follow before it starts [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:02:33]

sop_steps.title: Warn Before Free Time Expires
sop_steps.action: Alert the broker before the two hours run out, and use that window to start negotiating.
sop_steps.detail: Tell the broker the shipper has not loaded the truck yet and that detention starts if the shipper does not move in the next 20 minutes. This opens room to push for a higher rate [Pauline Nabacwa — fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:04:45]

sop_steps.title: Close Out With BOL and Invoice
sop_steps.action: Get in and out times initialed on the BOL, keep the gate tickets and photos, invoice, and follow up until the charge lands on settlement.
sop_steps.detail: Have someone at the facility write and initial the in and out times on the bill of lading, and photograph everything. Then submit the claim with the documentation attached [Think Trucking — uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:07:16]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is what happens when the shipper says no. ShipLeague's broker-side host is blunt: if you ask your customer for detention and the customer refuses, you still pay it, because the brokerage is the customer to the carrier and a shipper refusal is no excuse [OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:02:22]. Craig Bliss runs a brokerage the same way, paying carriers off the brokerage's own policy rather than the customer's, while admitting the common practice is to pay carriers only what the paying customer agreed to [WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:06:32]. Freightbrokerchic's guest Dexter takes the opposite line: as a carrier bills detention, the broker can only pay out what the customer has already authorized, and nobody reaches into their own pocket to lose money on a load [zvX7UreND4E @ 00:06:27]. Nate Cross at Freight 360 sits in the middle, carving out a messy zone where the customer refuses a TONU but the driver already rolled toward the pickup or turned down a good load, and the broker makes a judgment call to cover a small TONU out of pocket to protect a solid carrier relationship [7sfi19fbIzU @ 00:05:05]. For carriers, the payout depends on which of these three philosophies sits on the other end of the rate confirmation.

Whether accessorials are a profit line or a pass-through is the second fault line. Brandon Manney teaches brokers to ask every shipper what it pays for detention and layover, then quote the carrier less: in the worked example the shipper pays $200 an hour, the carrier is told $100, and on two hours the broker banks $200 while the driver never learns the shipper's number [8Mhf3iqBflw @ 00:03:47]. Manney frames layover the same way, collecting $500 and paying the trucking company $400 or even $300 depending on what it will accept. Freight 360 teaches the reverse: detention is invoiced directly to the customer and passed directly through to the carrier, with no additional profit made by the broker [A7rlv69JAj8 @ 00:02:31]. On the Final Mile podcast the Freight 360 hosts went further, describing an agent whose customer approved a TONU the carrier never requested and who planned to keep it, and telling that agent flatly it was the carrier's money for wasted time [xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:11:49]. Think Trucking flags the same leakage on the carrier side: some carriers pass detention straight to company drivers, others keep it or pay less, so a driver should get the pass-through policy in writing before sitting at a dock where the carrier might collect $60 an hour and pay out $20 [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:07:49].

Even the headline numbers are contested between camps. ShipLeague calls $50 an hour after two hours free the industry standard [OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:03:56]. Never Stop Trucking says the two-hour window only works in the shipper's and broker's favor because most trucks load in 30 minutes to an hour and a half, and treats $50 an hour as the bare minimum for idling equipment, burning fuel and a stranded driver [tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:03:38]. Pauline Nabacwa reports brokers offering $12, $15 or $20 an hour, or flat fees of $100 to $200, and calls it cheap change against the day lost. Layover bands swing wider still: Freightbrokerchic's guest pegs a customary $250 a day [zvX7UreND4E @ 00:04:50], Freight 360 says expect around $500 depending on equipment, and Brandon Manney says $500 to $1,000 or more. The TONU trigger splits as well. Never Stop Trucking says the common $150 is paid whether the driver deadheaded two miles or 200, but only once the truck physically reaches the pickup, not halfway there [tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:07:56]. Freight 360 instead pays when the driver is actively working the load, including one already rolling toward the shipper an hour before pickup, and expects the customer to cover around $200.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated firsthand loss is booking blind. Tim at Freight Master Resources walked a carrier friend through a first load with a Georgia brokerage: the driver arrived around 10:30 for a noon delivery, was told to take a nap, and at three o'clock learned the appointment was actually 6 a.m. the next morning, putting a hurricane relief pickup at risk while the broker ignored calls, emails, texts and Telegram [1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:02:28]. Neither the rate confirmation nor the carrier agreement mentioned detention or layover, so the broker threw roughly $150 and that was it [1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:04:16]. ShipLeague says it is literally rare for a dispatcher or driver to ask about detention while asking commodity, distance, weight and rate [OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:00:18]. Brandon Manney describes having to school callers who book off the load board without ever asking. On Final Mile, Freight 360 traced a carrier who checked in at 10 a.m. for a 5 p.m. pickup, sat until 9 p.m. with no product and bailed, back to nobody setting expectations, and named three things to settle before every pickup: what happens if it is not loaded on time, the detention terms, and the cutoff between detention and layover [xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:04:39].

The second trap is the clock itself. Think Trucking warns the two-hour grace is measured from appointment time, not arrival, so an hour spent waiting early may not count at all [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:01:10]. Never Stop Trucking reads three or four free hours on a rate confirmation as a big red flag that the broker already knows the shipper loads slowly, and adds that detention usually carries a cap, such as $50 an hour up to $250, after which a $250 layover works out to roughly $10 to $12 an hour [tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:05:33]. Freight 360 picked apart a case where a new broker moved an 8 a.m. delivery to 11 a.m. mid-load, the receiver could not start until noon, and the broker recognized detention only from 1 p.m., leaving one billable hour on a lost day. The hosts said they would have paid three hours from the original 8 a.m. appointment, and that most of the time this pattern is a broker lying to cover a hard load, then trying to stiff the carrier [xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:09:49]. They have also watched carriers file on a broker's bond, and told one of their own brokers to pay up because the bond would likely pay and the brokerage would owe it back [xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:08:07].

Even when the paperwork is clean, the economics stay thin. Pauline Nabacwa sent a truck 160 deadhead miles, sat until 9 p.m., watched the load cancel with no rebook that night or the next day, and the most the broker offered was $150 TONU [fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:07:53]. Pauline learned to reopen TONU terms the moment detention starts counting; on a later load that slid from noon to a 5 p.m. pickup, Pauline had warned the broker about a turn-away, the missing freight piece proved the point, and that earlier warning helped push the TONU to $540 [fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:09:13]. Alfa X Logistics tells dispatch clients it is realistically 50/50: half the time the money is collected, the other half the broker caves, stops responding, and little can be done unless the amount justifies legal action [CNjYZO0c1o4 @ 00:02:55]. Craig Bliss adds that most customers refuse detention when the broker got no heads-up before charges started, and that agents and mega brokerages tend to go MIA once detention is requested. The cost of losing it compounds: Think Trucking puts five lost hours a week at $60 an hour at $300 weekly, or $15,600 a year sitting still [uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:09:27].

callout.title: Do Not Roll Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Every loss above traces back to terms nobody wrote down, a clock nobody documented, or a TONU nobody renegotiated before the cancellation. Clear these four checks on every load before the truck moves.
items: No detention rate, free-time start and layover terms in the rate confirmation or carrier packet means no booking; a blank agreement left one carrier with roughly $150 [Freight Master Resources — 1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:04:16].
Three or four free hours on the rate confirmation is a red flag for a slow shipper, so price the sit into the rate or pass on the load [Never Stop Trucking — tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:04:56].

Run one email chain with a timestamped arrival notice, a pre-expiry warning, a detention-started notice and BOL in and out times before departure, because verbal calls prove nothing [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:02:33].
Once detention starts counting, reopen TONU terms before the load cancels instead of accepting a default $150 [Pauline Nabacwa — fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:08:53].

chapters.pull_quote: "A customer not paying it is no excuse for a broker not to pay it to a carrier." — ShipLeague (OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:03:10).
action_checklist: Before booking, ask the broker whether they pay detention, the hourly rate and after how many hours the clock starts, then make sure it is written into the rate confirmation [Trucking Territory — Q-HgB9nn1jI @ 00:04:12].

Read the broker carrier agreement instead of blanket signing it; if it is silent, send your own detention, layover and accessorial terms as a PDF or DocuSign for the broker to sign [Freight Master Resources — 1Fdc8KYk8M0 @ 00:07:18].
On arrival, email the broker the check-in time plus the exact time and hourly rate at which detention will start [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:02:33].

Send a warning before free time expires and a detention-started notice when it does, then add the broker's accounting team or operations staff to the same chain if nobody answers [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:04:36].
Get in and out times written on the bill of lading and initialed by someone at the facility, keep gate tickets and receipts, and photograph everything [Think Trucking — uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:07:00].

Brokers: ask every shipper its detention policy up front, send a detention approval email with the PO number when a truck is held, and issue an updated rate confirmation with the approved hours [Brandon Scott — V11p0IBJsTk @ 00:08:16].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I spot and prevent double brokering and carrier identity fraud before a load goes missing?
chapters.title: Double Brokering and Freight Fraud Defense
chapters.subtitle: How double brokering evolved, warning signs, carrier vetting with Highway, RMIS and Truckstop MFA, Carrier411 policy changes, attorney-led prevention, and new federal rules targeting fraudulent brokers
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Double Broker Bounty Hunter, Freight 360, Highway, Overdrive's Hank Seaton and ThinkFreight converge on one thesis: double brokering is now an identity-theft game, run through phished load board logins, look-alike email domains, dark-web DOT PINs and bought MC numbers, usually by one operator posing as both carrier and broker. Defense mechanics are concrete: Highway-style association insights that expose shared addresses, phones and equipment; a 20% off-market rate trigger; corporate-office callbacks on load number and lane; withheld PO numbers released only after geofenced photo checks; and carrier names on the bill of lading. Numbers frame the stakes: $2 to $3 billion in 2024 losses, a $75,000 bond that paid Convoy carriers under 10 cents on the dollar, and a 7-day bond replenishment rule enforced from January 16, 2026. Speakers split on rebrokering chain depth and Carrier411 reporting.

key_metrics.context: John Cana cites 2024 estimates of economic damage from double brokering alone, up from a half billion dollars in 2023 per FreightWaves and Triumph Pay, excluding stolen or ransomed cargo.

key_metrics.value: 20% above or below market triggers digging; 30% above is most likely a scam

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: John Cana, who runs the Double Broker Bounty Hunter channel, calls double brokering the root of every other freight crime, from cargo theft to ransomed cargo to nonpayment [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:02:15]. The playbook starts with a carrier identity. Scammers either file their own authority using a scrapyard VIN and a pencil-whipped DOT inspection from a bribed mechanic, phish a real carrier's setup packet by posting a fake load and sitting on those documents for as long as the insurance stays valid, or buy aged MC numbers that exiting carriers advertise on Facebook and X [J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:12:13]. The broker side mirrors it: forged rate confirmations doctored in Adobe, look-alike domains such as ship-abc swapped in for abclogistics, and fake DAT authentication emails that harvest load board credentials. Cana insists the chain is short, not a game of telephone: the same person who books from the real broker while posing as a carrier is usually the one posing as a broker to the real carrier, keeping a smoke screen in the middle [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:19:58]. Keep Loadings describes the street result in plain terms, with scammers buying old clean MC numbers and cloning legitimate carrier names to book high-value cargo and steal the entire trailer [FbcZES6peVA @ 00:01:42].

The vetting consensus centers on identity data that does not line up. Nate Cross of Freight 360 lists five red flags: no inspection history or unverifiable equipment, rates that sound too good to be true, email or phone details that do not match the FMCSA registration, PO box or residential addresses on a carrier offering to move multiple loads, and community reports from Highway, the TIA Watchdog list, or the Excel lists brokers pass between each other [gnxgKnnz6Jw @ 00:02:35]. Highway's demos show the same pattern in data form. One carrier with active authority and a recent inspection still carried eight insights: a residential address within a quarter mile of a carrier holding broker authority, a claim of 10 or more trucks, an inspection-to-truck ratio in the bottom 10 of its peer group, and shared phones, emails, contacts, an address and even a vehicle with a second carrier, which Highway calls two carriers sharing identities [b-vDBH9GpuA @ 00:01:33]. A second Highway walkthrough flagged a carrier self-reporting 16 trucks with zero inspections in 24 months and contact details reused across three active MC numbers [sKKld4Wdyqg @ 00:01:17]. Hank Seaton tells Overdrive listeners to start any fraud screen by looking for common addresses and common names [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:42:57].

Everyone agrees the losses are large and the federal backstop is thin. Cana cites FreightWaves and Triumph Pay putting 2023 double brokering damage at a half billion dollars, with 2024 estimates of $2 to $3 billion before stolen or ransomed cargo is counted [J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:10:19]. Bridge Logistics relays Carrier411 CEO Darren Brewer's figure of more than $100 million a year and warns that defrauded carriers chase shippers for payment while honest brokers end up paying the same load twice [uT4ymtB7YcA @ 00:01:49]. The $75,000 broker bond is treated as a floor, not protection: Cana notes some mega brokerages run bonds above $10 million, but when Convoy shut down with about $34 million in loads chasing a $75,000 bond, carriers collected less than 10 cents on the dollar [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:08:37]. ThinkFreight reports that since January 16, 2026, FMCSA can suspend a broker whose bond or trust falls below $75,000 and is not replenished within seven calendar days. Shortfalls can come from unpaid claims, a broker consenting to a drawdown, ignoring valid claim notices, or a claim turned into a federal court judgment, though the host, coming from a broker background, still wants bonds sized to freight volume [s-qzw5ZxjmU @ 00:01:41].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Cana's rate-confirmation forensics are the sharpest street mechanics on offer. The pricing test is a 20% rule: any load posted 20% above or below market gets heavy digging, 30% above market is most likely a scam no matter which broker is named, and a Minneapolis to Elk River post paying $2,500 for 32 miles was an instant scam call [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:14:19]. On paper, Cana checks whether the pro number font differs from the rest of the header, whether the email domain matches the real brokerage, and whether shipper and receiver codes are four-character alphanumerics, which signal an Amazon load that is a scam if it is not moving through the Relay app [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:24:56]. A Gmail address triggers questions every time; Cana has verified only two legitimate brokers using Gmail out of roughly 60,000. Behavioral tells include one-line rate cons with no fine print, a broker demanding the bill of lading at pickup, check-in instructions under another carrier's name, and status demands at arrival, check-in, loading, and paperwork. Freight 360's Nate Cross adds that a too-good rate usually means the carrier plans to rebroker, take quick pay, and vanish, leaving the broker to pay the second carrier again [gnxgKnnz6Jw @ 00:02:20].

For brokers, the working stack layers vetting software over physical proof. Nate Cross runs Highway at the Freight 360 brokerage for inspection history, registered equipment, community reports, and an ELD-fed map of equipment locations, then makes GPS tracking mandatory for the full load when fraud is suspected; most fraudsters quit once challenged for tracking or an ELD download before payment [uGu6NcZkt28 @ 00:01:57]. Cross also demands photos or video at the shipper showing equipment, the driver's face, registration, driver's license, and the MC on the truck door, zooming in for doctored images, and withholds the PO or pickup number until identity and location are confirmed. QuickScope automates that gate: the driver gets a text, takes a one-time photo inside a 2m geofence, and character recognition checks the company name, MC, and DOT before pickup details release automatically [uGu6NcZkt28 @ 00:03:45]. Hank Seaton estimates two-thirds to three-quarters of truckload shipments move without the carrier's name on the paperwork [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:25:28]. His protocol: put the authorized carrier's name on the bill of lading, send that name to the consignor at booking, show the contracting broker as the send-freight-bill-to party, and require the driver to present credentials, including a driver's license, satisfactory to the consignor [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:26:07].

Carriers get their own checklist. Cana tells them to call the corporate office of any medium or large brokerage, found through the DAT directory, to confirm the load number, the lane, and that they are listed as carrier of record; with small shops, ask the shipper which broker it uses, but never talk money, because that edges into back solicitation [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:29:21]. Cana also recommends drivers sign over a colored rubber stamp carrying the MC number, carrier name, and driver name, so a scammer cannot hide the real carrier or forge a clean receiver signature [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:11:25]. On onboarding, Cana walks dispatchers through the Truckstop MFA layered onto RMIS setups since January 2024: the owner completes a one-time ID check with a driver's license scan and selfie, then each setup needs an SMS, biometric, or authenticator code plus the usual emailed verification code, adding about 30 seconds once configured; delete cookies between setups or the flow hangs [aSSPaOdn5ZI @ 00:12:31]. Seaton adds a pressure valve: a carrier who suspects fraud mid-haul can insist on payment for delivery of the shipment, which Seaton frames as a possessory lien rooted in old commerce law [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:38:00].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The $75,000 broker bond is the loudest fault line. ThinkFreight, speaking from a broker background, calls the new FMCSA rule a slight step forward: a broker whose bond or trust drops below $75,000 and is not replenished within seven calendar days can be suspended, but the speaker argues the bond should scale with brokerage size, get reviewed every year, and that anyone moving a billion dollars in freight should carry far more than a replenishing minimum [s-qzw5ZxjmU @ 00:04:52]. John Cana of Double Broker Bounty Hunter pushes the same direction with harder numbers: some mega brokerages already run bonds upwards of $10 million while others still sit at $75,000, and when big brokers like Convoy shut down, carriers chasing roughly $34 million in loads against a $75,000 bond collected less than 10 cents on the dollar [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:08:37]. Attorney Hank Seaton, on Overdrive, describes a case where an operator ran up $1.9 million in carrier receivables, filed bankruptcy, and left 273 carriers with maybe four percent [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:20:28]. The split is about remedy, not diagnosis. ThinkFreight banks the seven-day replenishment trigger as progress, while Cana wants the bond itself sized to the freight a broker has on the road at any given time [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:09:20].

Practitioners also split on whether the federal government will fix this. The Commercial Carrier Journal guest argues the Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act would give the government teeth and funding to fine and even shut down fraudulent businesses, but insists it is just another tool in the tool belt that should not stop carriers from deploying technology and getting close with partners [u2IgQ87ZELQ @ 00:01:19]. Seaton goes the other way: the statute already lets the government charge a fraudster up to ten thousand dollars per violation, yet FMCSA has no appetite for it, complaints can wait as much as a year for a response, and the real fix is self-help, an agreement among brokers and carriers large and small to quit the sloppy procedures [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:17:45]. Cana lands in the middle. FMCSA believes court challenges blocked its civil penalty power, Cana disagrees with that interpretation, and private outfits like the bounty hunter program and the freight fraud task force are stepping in to help the agencies do their job [3WxrmhqpsyY @ 00:15:57]. ThinkFreight still calls enforcement of the financial responsibility rule a step forward, noting the rule took effect in January 2024 but enforcement was delayed until January 2026, with the broker transparency rulemaking expected next [s-qzw5ZxjmU @ 00:04:06].

Watchlists split the same camp. Freight 360's Nate Cross tells brokers that community reports on Highway or the TIA Watchdog list, plus Excel lists of internal double brokering reports passed from broker to broker, are a strong indicator to avoid a carrier [gnxgKnnz6Jw @ 00:04:01]. Cana is more skeptical, estimating at least 10 percent of Carrier411 reports are false or exaggerated, while co-host Jimmy argues a bad experience earns an internal do-not-use flag, not a Freight Guard that tells the world to drop Joe's Trucking [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:17:59]. Cana later blasted Carrier411 for making deleted Freight Guard reports permanent, growing from 12 to 26 report categories, and allowing reports against carriers who file on a broker's bond or threaten legal action, calling it a weapon brokers use to intimidate and extort carriers [o7UDt2VXwwU @ 00:01:28]. Quick pay draws the same kind of split. Cana tells brokers that a carrier demanding quick pay from a well-established broker, one every factor already covers, is a warning sign, but Jimmy counters that most brokers run quick pay cheaper than the five to three percent a factor charges, and that it helps new carriers factors will not take on, calling it a gamble but the price of doing business [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:20:11].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures Seaton walked through started with nobody checking who actually backed into the dock. In one case, two reputable broker-carriers tendered loads to a fraudster posing as a broker, the bills of lading at pickup never showed the actual carrier's name, and roughly three weeks later the parties realized the loads were copper wire in a scam of over $2.6 million; all seven loads had been reconsigned to an empty warehouse, and six months on nobody, including the FBI, FMCSA, and state police, could find the freight [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:22:34]. In another, over two dozen victims were scammed by an outfit FMCSA showed running only 60,000 miles, freight was claimed broken down at a Montana truck stop, seals came back broken and resealed, and the home office was a McMansion in Ohio [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:32:16]. Bridge Logistics describes the same endgame: the real carrier is sent to an unknown location and the product is transloaded onto another victimized carrier with a new bill of lading [uT4ymtB7YcA @ 00:02:31]. Cana's tell is silence. When dispatch goes dark after booking or tracking fails, the cargo is gone, and getting law enforcement to take cargo theft seriously remains the problem [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:18:48].

The economics of a single double-brokered load hit everyone twice. Nate Cross warns that when the fraudster collects and never pays the hauling carrier, the broker typically ends up paying for the same load twice, once to the fraudster and again to the carrier that actually moved it [gnxgKnnz6Jw @ 00:01:27]. Bridge Logistics adds that defrauded carriers go after shippers for payment when they cannot track down the fake broker, that legitimate brokers are commonly on the hook for multiple payments, and that the rates promised to double-brokered carriers run much higher than what the legitimate broker negotiated [uT4ymtB7YcA @ 00:01:09]. Seaton describes collection agencies that find a hoodwinked small carrier, take an assignment for 50 percent of whatever they collect, and hammer upstream, so the honest broker catches heat from the customer over a $3,000 demand on a load the broker never knew was double brokered [jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:15:35]. George of Truck Driver Nation frames the carrier's side: that money is fuel money, the only path back in most scenarios is to back source the load all the way to the original direct shipper and bill them, and speed matters because the fraudster is racing to collect first [5dP6IV7sJW0 @ 00:02:47].

Identity hijacks are the trap that compounds fastest. Cana warns that DOT PIN numbers compromised in the March 2023 data breach are for sale on the dark web, and that the minute a carrier discovers its information was pirated, the problem has existed for at least 24 hours with at least 100 loads double brokered in its name [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:17:23]. Scammers also post a fake load, award it to a real carrier, harvest the setup documents, and sit on them for as long as the insurance stays good, up to three months, before booking freight under that identity, while brokers get phished by fake DAT emails asking them to authenticate their accounts [J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:12:35]. Forged rate confirmations look clean at first glance: Cana caught a mismatched font on the pro number, lookalike domains such as brockb.net and logisticsdynamicsinc.com, and four-character alphanumeric shipper and receiver codes marking Amazon loads that only the relay app user gets paid on [3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:27:54]. The Commercial Carrier Journal guest expects the curve to get worse, since very advanced AI lets fraudsters scrape large amounts of data, fabricate details like physical location, and hide their actions much more effectively [u2IgQ87ZELQ @ 00:04:31].

callout.title: Stop Before The Load Moves
callout.body: Each check below comes straight from a loss or near-loss the practitioners reported; clear all four before releasing pickup details or cutting a carrier payment.
items: Confirm the carrier's DOT PIN has been reset since the March 2023 breach, because a compromised PIN lets a scammer file a fake MCS-150 and change all the SAFER contact information in a couple of minutes [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:13:35].

Never authenticate a load board account from an emailed link; DAT does not do that by email, and a phished login is the start of a very long nightmare [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:17:44].
Require the authorized carrier's name on the bill of lading, because in the copper wire scam the bills at pickup never showed who was actually hauling [Overdrive — jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:25:46].

Treat a carrier that goes dark after booking, or a tracking feed that fails, as a stolen load and escalate at once, because once they go dark the cargo is gone [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:18:48].

chapters.pull_quote: "The minute you find out you've had a problem, that problem's been there for at least 24 hours and you have at least a 100 loads double brokered in your name." — attributed to Double Broker Bounty Hunter (3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:17:23).
action_checklist: Open the Highway location, operation, and association insights on every new carrier and flag residential addresses near a broker authority, low inspection-to-truck counts, and shared phones, emails, or vehicles [Highway — b-vDBH9GpuA @ 00:01:33].

Make GPS tracking mandatory for the full load when fraud is suspected, start it before the truck heads to pickup, and demand an ELD download proving location before paying [Freight 360 — uGu6NcZkt28 @ 00:02:15].

Withhold the PO or pickup number until identity and location are verified, using QuickScope to text the driver for a one-time geofenced photo checked by character recognition for company name, MC, and DOT [Freight 360 — uGu6NcZkt28 @ 00:03:45].

Carriers: after receiving a rate confirmation from a medium or large broker, call the corporate number from the DAT directory to verify the load number, the lane, and that you are carrier of record [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:29:05].

Write into broker and shipper contracts that the bill of lading shows the authorized carrier and the broker as send freight bill to, and transmit that carrier's name to the consignor at booking [Overdrive — jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:26:07].

Issue drivers a color rubber stamp carrying the carrier MC number, carrier name, and driver name for every bill of lading signature so a scammer cannot hide who the real carrier is [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:11:25].

chapters.question_prompt: When cargo is lost or damaged, who is liable, what does insurance actually pay, and how do I file a claim?
chapters.title: Cargo Liability, Insurance and Claims
chapters.subtitle: Carmack Amendment and why it doesn't apply to brokers, carrier limits of liability, cargo vs. contingent cargo coverage and its gaps, contingent auto pricing, policy evidence requirements, and step-by-step claim filing
chapters.executive_summary: Freight brokerage practitioners agree on the liability map. Under the Carmack Amendment the motor carrier is automatically liable. Brokers sit outside Carmack and are governed by contract. A broker's contingent cargo policy only ever matches what the carrier already carries, and Freight 360 reports one contingent payout, $17,000, in 45 years at Peerless Road Warrior Logistics. The street mechanics are documentary: a written claim with a dollar figure and commercial invoice, the 30-day acknowledgment and 120-day disposition clocks, agent-emailed confirmation that excluded commodities are covered, and CIF-plus-10% valuation on international cargo. Carrier liability is a floor, and Cargolinked shows a $300,000 container returning about $22,000. The disagreements are over three questions: whether contingent is 'fake insurance' or a product that has come a long way, how long claimants really have to file, and whether shippers must prove carrier negligence.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every liability conversation starts with the Carmack Amendment, and the practitioners line up hard on who it hits. Transportation attorney Cassandra Gaines calls it the 'big fat cat' because it sits on top of state law and leaves motor carriers almost no wiggle room. The carrier is automatically liable, and the claimant only has to show three things: the goods were tendered in good condition on an un-notated bill of lading, they were delivered damaged or lost, and a commercial invoice backs the value [Ig6sI3O1a14 @ 00:11:37]. Brokers sit outside that box. Gaines states flatly that Carmack applies only to motor carriers and freight forwarders. For a broker, the governing law is the contract. If there is no paper, it is the oral agreement to arrange transportation. That is the line to throw back at an angry customer who insists the broker owns the claim [NyOX8UjzDAo @ 00:00:44]. TLI tells shippers the same thing from the 3PL seat. The motor carrier, not the broker, is the liable party, so the play is to maximize value with that carrier, file against it, and pass 100% of the settlement back to the shipper [fxzUlwnz1mE @ 00:00:52]. Cerasis frames the shipper's burden in three matching elements, citing Title 49 U.S. Code 14706: good-condition tender, damaged or unreasonably late delivery, and the dollar amount of the damages [mJw3vbSaJbw @ 00:03:54].

The second point of agreement is that contingent cargo is not primary coverage, whatever a customer's insurance requirement implies. Nate Cross of Freight 360 defines it as a secondary policy that depends on the carrier's primary cargo insurance already being in place. It is built as a safety net for the cases where that primary policy denies a claim or refuses to pay, and customers need to be told it is not a primary cargo policy [kAT7s21mZIE @ 00:01:33]. In the shorter Freight 360 clip the mechanics get blunter. The contingent policy only ever matches what the selected motor carrier already has. Take a $200,000 electronics load on a carrier with $100,000 in coverage and an electronics exclusion: it gets nothing from a broker's $250,000 contingent policy, even though that is exactly the scenario shippers think they are buying protection for [FtL-2SOSFOU @ 00:00:45]. The hosts name only rare triggers. One is a carrier policy lapsing mid-transit without anyone knowing. The other is the carrier's insurer folding or simply failing to respond. That is why they call contingent 'fake insurance' and a 'feel-good' for shipper management [FtL-2SOSFOU @ 00:02:14]. TLI lands in the same place. It describes contingent as cover for extreme outlier events, such as a carrier going bankrupt in the middle of a freight claim, and notes that not all commodities are covered [fxzUlwnz1mE @ 00:01:26].

Third, every practitioner who touches carrier liability treats it as a floor rather than real cover. Trade Risk Guaranty says carrier reimbursement generally covers only a fraction of the shipper's loss. Its prescription: the only way to ensure reimbursement for full value is to buy cargo insurance, which covers loss, damage, or theft between origin and final destination even when the carrier is at fault [pbs3U-vmpzM @ 00:03:18]. Cargolinked puts a number on the gap. A $300,000 container that goes overboard returns roughly $22,000 under the usual sea rules, about 7%, because carrier liability is capped by weight or package and never by value, and carriers still keep defenses like perils of the sea and poor packing [rbmdGEpBKCI @ 00:00:01]. The fourth shared baseline is that the paper a broker vets does not tell the whole story. Freight 360 points out that a certificate of insurance shows policy limits and coverage dates but does not always show the exclusions, which creates risk for both broker and customer. Freight 360 also says a cheap policy often has a ton of gaps [kAT7s21mZIE @ 00:03:00]. Jared Palmer of Epic Insurance Brokers is just as blunt. Good insurance costs money, cheap insurance and the best coverage are competitors, and a $50,000 premium that should have been $150,000 will not respond the way the buyer expects when the loss hits [xQYjaYAvyms @ 00:17:34].
